intro: say hook, why_it_matters, link_to_before, today_goal in that order. Keep it warm and short.

teaching_flow: each step has teacher_says (say these ideas, in the child's easy words), show (assets to display), ask_question_ids (ask these after teaching that step). Do not skip the teaching to jump to questions.
teaching_note and if_child_is_stuck are for the tutor. Use them when the child is wrong or stuck.
Judge answers ONLY with the rubric of that question (answer_key accept list, partial, incorrect). Never invent an answer. For mode 'open', use the correct, partial and incorrect descriptions.
On a wrong answer: give hint level 1, then 2, then 3 (hint_ids). If the wrong answer matches a misconception, use its response_text.
Use only the words and numbers in the card. Do not add new numbers. Fractions are spoken as words, for example '3 fourths'.
Do not use the symbols plus, minus, times, divide, equals in child text. Say the words.

assets_required lists pictures to build by code. status 'not_available' means no picture exists yet. If missing, describe in words only and keep the question answerable by voice.

objective.text: Explore volume by building with and counting unit cubes.

big_idea.text: Volume is the space a solid takes up. We count unit cubes to measure it.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The amount of space a solid takes up.
vocabulary.example: A box of 12 cubes has a volume of 12 cubic units.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A cube with edges of 1 unit. We use it to measure volume.
A cube with each edge 1 centimeter long.
One floor of cubes in a solid.

intro.hook: How much space does a block building take up? You count the blocks.
intro.why_it_matters: Volume tells you how much fits in a box or a room. It is useful every day.
intro.link_to_before: You know how to find the area of a flat shape.
intro.today_goal: Today you will measure the space a solid takes up by counting cubes.

teaching_flow.title: Build a building
teacher_says: Think of a building made of blocks. First you make the ground floor. Then you add a second floor. Then a third.
Today we count how much space a building like this takes up.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up: area
teacher_says: Area is the flat space inside a shape. We measure it in square units.
A 4 inch by 2 inch rectangle has an area of 8 square inches.
A 5 centimeter square has an area of 25 square centimeters.
Today we go from flat to solid.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 1: build up floor by floor
teacher_says: Picture a square on grid paper that has an area of 4 square units.
Put 4 cubes on it. That is the ground floor.
Add 4 more cubes on top. That is the second floor. There are 8 cubes.
The ground did not change. We built up, not out. The solid got taller, not wider.
Add one more floor of 4. Now there are 12 cubes. Count it as 3 fours, or 3 times 4.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many cubes are on one floor? How many floors? Say the total.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 2: what is volume and what is its unit?
teacher_says: A cube with each edge 1 centimeter long is called a cubic centimeter.
Volume is the amount of space a solid takes up.
We use squares to measure area. We use cubes to measure volume. These are cubic units.
2 cubes together have a volume of 2 cubic centimeters. 4 cubes in a square have a volume of 4 cubic centimeters.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source writes 'cubic unit', 'cubic centimeter', and cm3 on the board. Say 'cubic centimeters' out loud. Keep the word volume in every answer.

teaching_flow.title: Different shapes, same volume
teacher_says: You can build many different solids from the same number of cubes.
With 4 cubes you can make a flat square. You can make a long row. You can make an L shape.
They look different. They all have a volume of 4 cubic centimeters. The same works with 5 cubes and 6 cubes.

teaching_flow.title: Drawing solids and hidden cubes
teacher_says: We draw solids on dot paper in 3D. A drawing shows the front, the top and one side.
In a drawing, some cubes can be hidden behind or under others. A drawing can fool you.
Joyce counted only the cubes she saw. She missed hidden ones. John drew 4 cubes for a volume of 5. His drawing is fine. One cube is hidden.
A bottom layer has 6 cubes. A second layer of 6 covers it. The volume is 12.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is holding up the top cube? Is there a cube under it?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Hands-on drawing on isometric dot paper is not tutorable. Use the picture and talk about hidden cubes instead.

source_ref.section: Concept Development, Problem 3; Student Debrief; Exit Ticket

teaching_flow.title: Jackie and Ron
teacher_says: Jackie and Ron each have 12 cubes. Jackie builds a tower 6 cubes high and 2 cubes wide. Ron builds a flat shape 6 cubes long and 2 cubes wide.
Jackie says hers has more volume because it is taller. Ron says they are the same. Who is right?
Ron is right. Both use 12 cubes. Volume counts cubes, not height.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Volume is the space a solid takes up. We count unit cubes. Same cubes means same volume. Watch out for hidden cubes.

explanations.title: What volume is
explanations.text: Volume is the amount of space a solid takes up. We measure it by counting unit cubes that fill the solid. The unit is a cubic unit, such as a cubic centimeter.

explanations.title: Building up, not out
explanations.text: When you add a floor on top, the solid gets taller. The base stays the same. The volume goes up by the number of cubes in the new floor.

explanations.title: Same cubes, same volume
explanations.text: Different shapes can be built from the same cubes. If the number of cubes is the same, the volume is the same. Height alone does not decide volume.

explanations.title: Hidden cubes in drawings
explanations.text: A drawing of a solid can hide cubes behind or under other cubes. Think about what is holding up the top cubes. Count the hidden cubes too.

examples.title: Three floors of 4
examples.text: Ground floor 4 cubes. Second floor 4 more makes 8. Third floor 4 more makes 12. Volume is 12 cubic centimeters.

examples.title: Jackie and Ron
examples.text: Jackie: tower 6 high and 2 wide. Ron: flat 6 long and 2 wide. Each has 12 cubes. Same volume.

questions.text: A rectangle is 4 inches by 2 inches. What is its area?
A square has sides of 5 centimeters. What is its area?
A ground floor has 4 cubes. We put 4 more cubes on top to make a second floor. How many cubes now?
Did the second floor change the ground floor? Does the solid take up more room on the ground?
We add one more floor of 4 cubes. How many cubes in all? Say the total.
There are 3 floors with 4 cubes each. Tell me a multiplication story for 12.
What if there were 5 floors with 4 cubes on each floor? How many cubes?
A cube has each edge 1 centimeter long. What do we call this cube?
Two of these cubes are together. What is their volume?
4 cubes sit in a square formation. What is the volume of the 4 cubes together?
We use squares to measure area. What do we use to measure volume?
In your own words, what is volume?
Can two solids that look different both have a volume of 4 cubic centimeters?
A row of 5 cubes has what volume?
In a drawing of a solid, can some cubes be hidden from view?
John draws a solid with a volume of 5 cubic centimeters. He draws only 4 cubes. Can his drawing be right?
A solid has a bottom layer of 6 cubes. A second layer of 6 cubes covers it exactly. What is the volume?
Jackie builds a tower 6 cubes high and 2 cubes wide. Ron builds a flat shape 6 cubes long and 2 cubes wide. Each uses 12 cubes. Who has the greater volume?
Why do the two structures have the same volume?
What do you need to think about when you count cubes in a drawing?

hints.text: Count the cubes one by one. Do not forget the cubes in the layer below.
Count how many cubes are in one layer. Then count the layers.
Each floor has the same number of cubes. Add that number again for each floor.
Squares measure flat area. Cubes measure space inside a solid.
Some cubes are hidden behind or under others. Think about what holds the top cubes up.
Same number of cubes means same volume, even if the shape looks different.
The cube has an edge of 1 centimeter. What is that cube called?

misconceptions.label: Thinks taller means more volume
misconceptions.description: Jackie said her tower has more volume because it is taller. Both structures use the same cubes.
detection_signals: child says the taller one is bigger
child compares height only
misconceptions.response_text: Count the cubes in each. Same cubes, same volume. A taller shape can be narrower.

misconceptions.label: Counts only the cubes you can see
misconceptions.description: Joyce counted only the cubes shown and missed hidden cubes. A drawing can hide cubes.
detection_signals: child counts only the front cubes
child says a drawing of 4 cubes cannot have volume 5
misconceptions.response_text: A drawing can hide cubes. Ask what holds up the top cubes. Think about the layers.

misconceptions.label: Uses square units for volume
misconceptions.description: Child gives volume in square centimeters, as for area.
detection_signals: child says square centimeters for volume
child says volume is in squares
misconceptions.response_text: Area uses flat squares. Volume uses cubes. So the unit is cubic centimeters.

We measure volume with cubes. The unit is a cubic unit.
Same number of cubes means same volume.

wrap_up.mental_model: Count the cubes in every floor, and the ones you cannot see.
wrap_up.closing_question: Say what volume means and what unit we use.

objective.text: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism by packing with cubic units and counting.

big_idea.text: Pack a box with cubes. Count one layer, then count the layers.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A solid shaped like a box.
The number of unit cubes that fill a solid.
vocabulary.example: A box of 8 cubes has a volume of 8 cubic units.

vocabulary.kid_definition: One flat floor of cubes in a box.
vocabulary.example: The bottom layer of box C has 16 cubes.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A flat pattern that folds up into a solid.
vocabulary.example: A box pattern on grid paper.

intro.hook: How many small cubes fit in a box? You can find out by packing it.
intro.why_it_matters: Boxes, rooms and tanks all have volume. Packing is the first way to find it.
intro.link_to_before: You counted cubes in solids and learned that volume is measured in cubic units.
intro.today_goal: Today you will pack boxes with cubes and find a faster way to count them.

teaching_flow.title: Packing a box
teacher_says: Imagine a gift box. How many small cubes fit inside?
Today we pack boxes with cubes. Then we learn a shortcut.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up: area and one cube
teacher_says: Area is the flat space in a shape. We use square units.
A rectangle 8 feet by 2 feet has an area of 16 square feet.
A square with sides of 4 meters has an area of 16 square meters.
Volume is different. One cube with an edge of 1 centimeter has a volume of 1 cubic centimeter.

source_ref.section: Fluency Practice: Find the Area; Find the Volume

teaching_flow.title: Box A: pack and count
teacher_says: Look at the flat pattern. The shaded part is the bottom. The flaps fold up to make the sides.
We fold it into a box, then fill it with cubes.
Box A has 4 cubes on the bottom. A second layer of 4 sits on top.
We can count one by one. We can count by twos. We can count by fours.
Four and four make 8 cubes. The volume of box A is 8 cubic centimeters.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many cubes on the bottom? How many layers? Count by fours.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source has students cut, fold and tape a net. That cannot be done here. The tutor shows the net and the folded box. The base 2 by 2 is rebuilt from the students' answers.

teaching_flow.title: Box B: the volume doubles
teacher_says: Box B is a longer box. The bottom is twice as long. It still has 2 layers.
The bottom has 8 cubes. Two layers of 8 make 16.
The volume went from 8 to 16. It doubled.
Why? Box B is like two box A side by side. The height did not change.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what changed, the bottom or the height? What stayed the same?

teaching_flow.title: Box C: predict without packing
teacher_says: For box C, we only pack the first layer. We do not cut and fold.
The bottom is 4 cubes by 4 cubes. That is 16 cubes.
The flaps show how many layers. Box C has 3 layers.
Sixteen, double is 32, and another 16 makes 48.
Sixteen times 3 is 48. The volume of box C is 48 cubic centimeters.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what does one layer hold? How many layers do the flaps show?

teaching_flow.title: Try other boxes
teacher_says: Now try other boxes. First find the bottom. Then count the layers.
Every layer has the same number of cubes. So we repeat the bottom for each layer.
Watch the unit. Volume is in cubic centimeters.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Hands-on net making with grid paper is not tutorable. Numbers are generated because the figures were stripped.

teaching_flow.title: Same volume, different boxes
teacher_says: A box pattern holds 24 cubes. Other patterns can also hold 24 cubes.
If the bottom has 8 cubes, there are 3 layers.
If the bottom has 12 cubes, there are 2 layers.

teaching_flow.title: How we packed
teacher_says: Think about how you packed. Cube by cube is slow. Layer by layer is fast.
Know the bottom layer and the layers. Then you can predict the volume.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Volume is how many cubes pack a box. Count the bottom layer, then count the layers.

explanations.title: Volume by packing
explanations.text: The volume of a box is the number of unit cubes that fill it. We measure it in cubic units, such as cubic centimeters.

explanations.title: Layers make packing fast
explanations.text: Pack one layer on the bottom and count it. Then count the layers. Every layer has the same number of cubes.

explanations.title: What the flaps show
explanations.text: In a flat box pattern, the shaded part is the bottom. The flaps stand up and show the height in layers.

explanations.title: When the bottom doubles
explanations.text: The bottom holds twice the cubes. The layers stay the same. So the volume doubles. Box B holds twice what box A holds.

examples.title: Box A and box B
examples.text: Box A has 4 on the bottom and 2 layers, so 8. Box B has 8 on the bottom and 2 layers, so 16. The volume doubled.
examples.display: A: 4 x 2 = 8 cubic cm; B: 8 x 2 = 16 cubic cm

examples.title: Box C
examples.text: The bottom is 4 by 4, so 16 cubes. The flaps show 3 layers. Sixteen times 3 is 48. The volume is 48 cubic centimeters.

questions.text: A rectangle is 8 feet long and 2 feet wide. What is its area?
A square has sides of 4 meters. What is its area?
Each small cube has an edge of 1 centimeter. What is its volume?
Box A holds a bottom of 4 cubes and 2 layers. We pack it with cubes. What is the volume of box A?
One way to pack box A is 4 on the bottom and 4 on top. How many layers is that?
Box A has 4 cubes in each layer. Count by fours. What is the last number?
Box B has a bottom twice as long as box A. It has the same 2 layers. What is its volume?
How many cubes are on the bottom of box B?
How does the volume of box B compare with box A? Say one word.
Why did the volume double from box A to box B?
In a flat box pattern, what do the flaps show us?
Box C has a bottom of 16 cubes, and its flaps show 3 layers. Predict its volume.
Box C is 4 cubes by 4 cubes on the bottom. How many cubes is that in the first layer?
Double 16 is 32. Then add another 16. What do you get? This is box C.
Can we find the volume of a box without filling the whole box?
A box has a bottom of 16 cubes and 2 layers. What is its volume?
A box has a bottom of 5 cubes and 4 layers. What is its volume?
A cube box has a bottom of 9 cubes and 3 layers. What is its volume?
A box pattern holds 24 cubes. Its bottom has 8 cubes. How many layers does it have?
Another box also holds 24 cubes. Its bottom has 12 cubes. How many layers?
We can pack a box cube by cube, row by row, or layer by layer. Which way is fastest for a big box?
Could you predict the volume of box C with fewer cubes than 48?
How has your idea of volume changed since the last lesson?

objective.text: Compose and decompose right rectangular prisms using layers.

big_idea.text: A prism is a stack of equal layers. We can cut layers three ways. The volume stays the same.

vocabulary.kid_definition: One flat group of cubes in a solid.
To break a solid into smaller parts.
To put parts together to make a solid.
vocabulary.example: Stack 3 layers of 9 to make a cube.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The number of unit cubes that fill a solid.
vocabulary.example: A prism of 60 cubes has a volume of 60 cubic centimeters.

intro.hook: How many ice cubes are in a stack of trays? Count by layers.
intro.why_it_matters: Layers help us count big solids fast. Boxes and buildings have layers too.
intro.link_to_before: You packed boxes and counted a bottom layer, then the layers.
intro.today_goal: Today you cut prisms into layers three ways. You find the volume each way.

teaching_flow.title: Stack of trays
teacher_says: Picture an ice cube tray with two rows of 8 cubes. Now picture 12 of those trays stacked up.
How many ice cubes in the whole stack? Each tray is a layer.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many cubes in one tray? How many trays?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The source asks students to draw a picture. The tutor shows the stack and asks the child to say the answer.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up
teacher_says: Volume is the number of cubes that fill a solid. We count in cubic centimeters.
We can also count by layers. A layer is one flat group of cubes.

teaching_flow.title: Build a 2 by 2 by 5 prism
teacher_says: Start with 4 cubes in a square, stacked 2 high. The volume is 4 cubic centimeters.
Add another layer next to it. The volume is 8. Add 3 more layers. The volume is 20.
Eight and twelve make 20. There are 5 layers of 4.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many cubes in one layer? Add that again for each new layer.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source has children build with real cubes. The tutor shows the pictures.

teaching_flow.title: Three ways to make layers
teacher_says: Imagine cutting the prism three ways.
Cut like bread slices, straight up and down. That makes 5 layers of 4. Five times 4 is 20.
Cut flat like cake layers. That makes 2 layers of 10. Two times 10 is 20.
Cut front and back. That makes 2 layers of 10. Two times 10 is 20.
The layers change. The volume does not.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: which way did we cut? How many layers? How many cubes in each?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source builds a table with the three decompositions. The tutor can read the table: 5 layers of 4, 2 layers of 10, 2 layers of 10.

teaching_flow.title: A cube from layers of 9
teacher_says: Build one layer that is 3 cubes by 3 cubes. It holds 9 cubes.
Cover it with another layer. Now there are 2 layers of 9. That is 18.
Add a third layer. Now there are 3 layers of 9. That is 27.
The shape is now a cube.

teaching_flow.title: A 3 by 4 by 5 prism
teacher_says: Now look at a prism that is 3 wide, 4 long and 5 high. Picture the bottom layer.
The bottom layer is 3 rows of 4 cubes. That is 12 cubes. It is 1 cube high.
The prism has 5 layers like it. Five times 12 is 60. The volume is 60 cubic centimeters.
We can cut it other ways. Three layers of 20 also make 60. Four layers of 15 make 60 too.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many cubes in the bottom layer? How many layers?

teaching_flow.title: Stacking equal layers
teacher_says: Marcos has a flat prism, 1 inch by 5 inches by 5 inches. One layer holds 25 cubic inches.
If he stacks more equal layers, the volume grows by 25 each time.
Meters work the same way. We can cut a prism into layers 1 meter high. We count cubic meters in each layer.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Problem Set figures were stripped. These numbers come from the Problem Set text. Child text writes cubic units with words.

teaching_flow.title: Same volume, different layers
teacher_says: Stephen and Chelsea want to add 72 cubic centimeters to a prism.
Chelsea adds 8 layers. Each layer has 9 cubes. Eight times 9 is 72.
Stephen adds only 4 layers. So each of his layers is bigger.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: if you use fewer layers, must each layer be bigger or smaller?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The prism figure is stripped. Layer sizes of 9 and 18 are rebuilt from 72 split into 8 and 4 layers.

teaching_flow.title: Looking back
teacher_says: Think about which layers are hardest to see. Front and back layers can be hard.
You can turn the prism or draw lines to help. You can think of a stack of ice trays too.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: A prism is a stack of equal layers. Count one layer. Then count the layers.
You can cut layers three ways. The volume stays the same.

explanations.title: What a layer is
explanations.text: A layer is one flat group of cubes. In a prism, every layer in a set has the same number of cubes.

explanations.title: Three ways to layer
explanations.text: We can cut a prism three ways. Cut it like bread slices, like cake layers, or front and back. Each way gives a different layer size.

explanations.title: Volume stays the same
explanations.text: Cutting does not add or remove cubes. We only group the cubes a new way. So the volume is the same.

explanations.title: Layers repeat
explanations.text: When all layers are equal, we multiply. Cubes in one layer times the number of layers gives the volume.

explanations.title: Ice tray stack
explanations.text: A stack of ice trays is a layered solid. Each tray is a layer of 16 cubes. Twelve trays give 192 cubes.

examples.title: The 2 by 2 by 5 prism
examples.text: Bread slices: 5 layers of 4. Cake layers: 2 layers of 10. Front and back: 2 layers of 10. Each way gives 20 cubic centimeters.

examples.title: The 3 by 4 by 5 prism
examples.text: The bottom layer is 3 by 4, so 12 cubes. There are 5 layers. Five times 12 is 60 cubic centimeters.

examples.title: Ice tray stack
examples.text: One tray has 2 rows of 8, so 16. There are 12 trays. Sixteen times 12 is 192 ice cubes.

questions.text: Six cubes sit in a solid. Each cube is 1 cubic centimeter. What is the volume?
A box has 4 cubes on the bottom and 3 layers. How many cubes is that?
An ice tray has two rows of 8 cubes. How many ice cubes are in one tray?
A stack has 12 of these trays. How many ice cubes are in the stack?
In the ice tray stack, what is one layer? Say it in a few words.
We build 4 cubes in a square, stacked 2 high. What is the volume?
We add one more layer of 4 cubes next to the first. What is the volume now?
We add 3 more layers next to the first two. What is the volume now?
We cut the prism like bread slices into vertical layers. How many layers are there?
Each bread slice layer has 4 cubes. There are 5 layers. What is the volume?
Now cut the same prism flat, like cake layers. It is 2 units high. How many cubes in each layer?
Is the volume still 20 cubic centimeters when we slice it flat?
One more way is front layers and back layers. There are 2 layers of 10. What is the volume?
We name the three ways bread slices, cake layers, and front and back. Do all three give the same volume?
A layer is 3 cubes by 3 cubes. What is the volume of one layer?
We cover it exactly with a second layer of 9. What is the volume now?
We add a third layer of 9. What is the volume now?
What is the overall shape of this prism? Its length, width and height are all 3.
A prism is 3 cubes wide, 4 cubes long, and 5 high. How many cubes are in the bottom layer?
The prism has 5 layers of 12 cubes. What is the volume?
Slice the 3 by 4 by 5 prism another way. There are 3 layers of 20 cubes. What is the volume?
Marcos makes a prism 1 inch by 5 inches by 5 inches. How many cubic inches is one layer?
Marcos stacks 4 equal layers. What is the volume in cubic inches?
Marcos stacks 7 equal layers. What is the volume in cubic inches?
A prism is 6 meters long, 4 meters tall, and 2 meters wide. We cut flat layers 1 meter high. How many layers?
Each flat layer is 6 meters by 2 meters. How many cubic meters in each layer?
What is the volume of the whole prism? It is 6 by 4 by 2 meters.
Stephen and Chelsea want to add 72 cubic centimeters. Chelsea adds 8 layers of 9 each. How many cubes is that?
Stephen adds 4 layers instead. How many cubes must each of his layers hold to make 72?
Why can both Stephen and Chelsea be right? Say it in a short answer.
Which layers are hardest to see? How can you make them easier?
How is a stack of ice trays like a prism with layers? How is it different?

objective.text: Use multiplication to calculate volume.

big_idea.text: Volume is length times width times height. It is also base area times height. The unit is cubic.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The area of the face that sits on the bottom.
vocabulary.example: A 3 by 2 face has a base area of 6 square centimeters.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The side that tells how many layers there are.
vocabulary.example: A prism with 4 layers has a height of 4.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The unit for volume. Three length units multiplied give it.
One flat side of a solid.

intro.hook: Counting every cube takes a long time. Is there a faster way?
intro.why_it_matters: Builders and packers find volume by multiplying. It is quick and exact.
intro.link_to_before: You counted layers of cubes and used layers three ways.
intro.today_goal: Today you will see that volume is length times width times height.

teaching_flow.title: Karen's mistake
teacher_says: Karen says a 2 by 2 by 1 prism has volume 5 cubic centimeters.
She added the sides. Is she right? Let us count the cubes.
The prism has 2 cubes in a row and 2 rows. That is 4 cubes in one layer. It has 1 layer.
The volume is 4 cubic centimeters. Karen should multiply, not add.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many cubes in one layer? How many layers?

teaching_flow.title: Warm up: area
teacher_says: Area is the flat space in a face. Multiply length by width.
A square with sides of 10 centimeters has an area of 100 square centimeters.
A rectangle 13 feet by 3 feet has an area of 39 square feet.

teaching_flow.title: Face area and layers
teacher_says: Look at a prism that is 3 centimeters long, 2 wide and 4 high.
The top face is 3 by 2. That is 6 square centimeters. It holds 6 cubes.
The area of the face matches the cubes in one layer.
Under that face are 4 layers. The height tells us the layers.
Multiply the face area by the height. Six times 4 is 24. The volume is 24 cubic centimeters.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is the area of the top face? Which side is not in that face?

teaching_flow.title: Square units become cubic units
teacher_says: Area uses square units. After we multiply by one more length, the unit becomes cubic.
Three length units multiplied give cubic units. Cubes measure space in three directions.

teaching_flow.title: Any face can be the base
teacher_says: We can use another face. The end face is 4 by 2. Its area is 8. There are 3 layers beside it. Eight times 3 is 24.
The front face is 3 by 4. Its area is 12. The width is 2. Twelve times 2 is 24.
All three ways give 24. We just multiplied the three sides in a different order.
So the volume is length times width times height.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source says the words face and base can be used for the same face on a right rectangular prism. Turn the prism so that face is the bottom.

teaching_flow.title: A shorter prism
teacher_says: Make the prism one layer shorter. It is now 3 by 2 by 3. We take away one layer of 6.
Six times 3 is 18. Or 24 take away 6 is 18.
The pattern holds. We can multiply the sides.

teaching_flow.title: When the area is given
teacher_says: Sometimes we get only the face area. A top face has an area of 4 square centimeters. The height is 4 centimeters.
Four layers of 4 give 16 cubic centimeters.
We do not need the sides of the face. The area and the other side are enough.
Try 6 square inches and 2 inches. Then try 3 square meters and 3 meters.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: which number is the area? Which number tells the layers?

teaching_flow.title: Practice with whole boxes
teacher_says: Tyron's box is 10 cm by 7 cm by 8 cm. We multiply all three sides.
Use the formula. Volume is length times width times height.
You can also use the face area and the height.

teaching_flow.title: What if the sides change?
teacher_says: Tyron changes his box. We see what happens to the volume.
Doubling one side doubles the volume. Halving one side halves it. Doing both makes no change.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: To find volume, multiply length, width and height. Or multiply the face area by the side left over.
The answer is in cubic units.

explanations.title: Volume by multiplying
explanations.text: The volume of a rectangular prism is length times width times height. Write it as V equals l times w times h.

explanations.title: Base area times height
explanations.text: The area of one face is the cubes in one layer. The side left over is the number of layers. Multiply them.

explanations.title: Why cubic units
explanations.text: Three length units multiplied give cubic units. Cubes measure space in three directions.

explanations.title: Any face can be the base
explanations.text: Turn the prism so any face sits on the bottom. The side left over is the height. The volume stays the same.

explanations.title: When the area is given
explanations.text: If you know the face area and the side left over, multiply them. You do not need length and width.

objective.text: Use multiplication to connect volume as packing with volume as filling.

big_idea.text: Packing and filling give the same volume. One cubic centimeter equals one milliliter.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A small amount of liquid. Its volume is 1 cubic centimeter.
A liquid unit. One liter is 1,000 milliliters.
How much liquid a container can hold.
How deep the water is, from the top down to the bottom.

intro.hook: How much water does a fish tank hold? You can find out with math.
intro.why_it_matters: Cooks, doctors and pool workers measure liquid volume every day.
intro.link_to_before: You multiply length, width and height to find volume.
intro.today_goal: Today you will link packing cubes with filling water.

teaching_flow.title: Packing and filling
teacher_says: There are two ways to see how much a box holds. We can pack it with cubes. We can fill it with water.
Today we link them. We find out how cubic centimeters and milliliters are related.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up
teacher_says: We count by 100 milliliters. When we reach 1,000 milliliters, we say 1 liter.
A 6 cm by 4 cm rectangle has an area of 24 square centimeters.
A 4 by 5 by 2 cm prism has a volume of 40 cubic centimeters.

teaching_flow.title: Packing and filling a box
teacher_says: Take a small box. We can find its volume in two ways.
Pack: fill it with cubes and count. Or multiply the three sides.
Fill: pour in water and measure it in milliliters.
One group packed 36 cubes. It also held 36 milliliters of water.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source is a hands-on exploration with boxes, cubes, water and a graduated cylinder. The tutor reports the results and asks the child to think about them.

teaching_flow.title: 1 cubic centimeter is 1 milliliter
teacher_says: Fill a graduated cylinder to 15 milliliters. Add 1 more milliliter. The level goes up to 16.
Now drop in one centimeter cube. The level goes up 1 milliliter again.
The cube did not add water. It pushed the water up.
So 1 cubic centimeter equals 1 milliliter. The number does not change.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how far did the level rise for 1 mL? How far for 1 cube?

teaching_flow.title: A big tank
teacher_says: A tank is 30 cm by 20 cm by 40 cm. It is full of water.
The water fills the whole tank. So the water volume is the tank volume.
Multiply 30, 20 and 40. That is 24,000 cubic centimeters.
One cubic centimeter equals one milliliter. So there are 24,000 milliliters.
One liter is 1,000 milliliters. So 24,000 milliliters is 24 liters.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is the volume of the tank? What stays the same when we change to mL?

teaching_flow.title: A fish tank, full and not full
teacher_says: A small fish tank is 15 cm by 10 cm by 10 cm. It is full. The volume is 1,500 cubic centimeters. That is 1,500 milliliters.
After a week, some water dries up. Now the water is 9 cm deep.
The tank did not change. The bottom is the same. Only the water height changed.
Multiply 15 by 10 by 9. That is 1,350 milliliters.
Another way: 1 cm of water went away. That is 150 milliliters. 1,500 take away 150 is 1,350.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is the depth of the water now? Does the bottom change?

teaching_flow.title: More tank problems
teacher_says: Use the water depth, not the tank height. A tank can be only part full.
To fill to the top, find the full volume. Then take away what is there. Or find the missing layer.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source tank numbers 26, 20, 18 and 15 come from Problem 6 of the Problem Set. Answers are computed.

teaching_flow.title: Cubes and milliliters in use
teacher_says: Cubes in a container tell us the water it holds. 30 cubes means 30 milliliters.
A bigger amount of water does not fit in a smaller container. Check the volumes.
A box 10 cm on every side holds 1,000 cubic centimeters. That is 1 liter.

teaching_flow.title: Looking back
teacher_says: Doctors say cc for cubic centimeter. One cc is one milliliter.
Water depth is the same idea as height for the water.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Packing counts cubes. Filling measures liquid. They match.
One cubic centimeter equals one milliliter. One thousand milliliters make 1 liter.

explanations.title: Volume as packing and as filling
explanations.text: Packing counts cubes that fit inside. Filling measures the liquid a container holds. Both tell the volume.

explanations.title: One cubic centimeter equals one milliliter
explanations.text: A 1 centimeter cube pushes the water up 1 milliliter. So 1 cubic centimeter equals 1 milliliter. The number stays the same.

explanations.title: Milliliters and liters
explanations.text: One liter is 1,000 milliliters. Divide milliliters by 1,000 to get liters. Multiply liters by 1,000 to get milliliters.

explanations.title: Water depth is height
explanations.text: When a tank is only part full, the water forms a prism. Its base is the tank bottom. Its height is the water depth.

objective.text: Find the total volume of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping rectangular prisms.

big_idea.text: Find the volume of each prism. Then add them. A tape diagram helps with part and whole problems.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A solid made of two or more prisms joined together.
vocabulary.example: Two boxes glued side by side.

vocabulary.kid_definition: Parts that share no space inside.
A bar picture that shows parts and a whole.
vocabulary.example: One long bar split into 3 units.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The volume of two or more parts put together.

intro.hook: A shed, a step and a chimney can all be one building made of boxes.
intro.why_it_matters: Real objects are often made of several boxes. You can find their volume by parts.
intro.link_to_before: You find the volume of one box by multiplying.
intro.today_goal: Today you will find the total volume of two joined prisms.

teaching_flow.title: Storage units
teacher_says: A storage company sells three units. The Cube has a volume of 64 cubic meters.
The Double has twice that volume. The Half has half that volume.
A cube has three equal sides. Four times 4 times 4 is 64. So each edge is 4 meters.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source asks what the dimensions could be and how to orient them for the most floor or the most height. The tutor uses volumes only. Possible sizes: the Double 4 by 4 by 8 and the Half 4 by 4 by 2.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up
teacher_says: We find volume by multiplying. A 3 by 4 by 2 prism has a volume of 24 cubic centimeters.
Know the volume and two sides? Divide to find the third side.

teaching_flow.title: Join two prisms
teacher_says: Partner A builds a 3 by 2 by 2 prism. It has 12 cubes.
Partner B builds a cube with edge 2. It has 8 cubes.
Join them any way you like. The total is 12 plus 8, which is 20 cubic units.
If we join them a new way, the total does not change. The parts stay the same.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is each part's volume? Add them.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source builds with real cubes. The tutor shows the picture.

teaching_flow.title: Two equal prisms
teacher_says: A prism is 3 meters by 2 meters by 7 meters. Its volume is 42 cubic meters.
Glue an identical prism to it. Add 42 and 42, or double 42. The total is 84 cubic meters.

teaching_flow.title: Two different boxes: find a missing side
teacher_says: Now the two boxes are different. There are many numbers on the picture. Use the right ones.
The bottom box has a volume of 120 cubic inches.
The top box has no width shown. It lines up with the bottom box. So its width is also 5 inches.
The top box has a volume of 30 cubic inches. Add 120 and 30 to get 150 cubic inches.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: which side of the top box lines up with the bottom box?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The Problem 3 figure was stripped. Only the volumes 120 and 30 and the width 5 are known from the teacher's words.

teaching_flow.title: Find a side by taking away
teacher_says: Now a bracket of 4 meters spans both boxes. The top box has no measures.
The bottom edge is 6 meters. The top box sticks out 4 meters. So the other part is 6 take away 4, which is 2 meters.
The width of the top box is 2 meters. Each box is 2 meters high.
The top box is 2 by 2 by 2. That is 8 cubic meters. The bottom box is 6 by 2 by 2. That is 24.
The total volume is 8 plus 24, which is 32 cubic meters.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is the whole length? What part is already known? Subtract.

teaching_flow.title: A tape diagram
teacher_says: Two prisms have a combined volume of 135 cubic meters. Prism A is double Prism B.
Draw two bars. Prism B is 1 unit. Prism A is 2 units. A bracket shows 135 for both.
That is 3 units in all. 135 divided by 3 is 45. So B is 45 and A is 90.
Prism A has a face area of 10 square meters. Its height is 90 divided by 10, which is 9 meters.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many equal units are there in all? Divide the total by that number.

teaching_flow.title: Problem Set practice
teacher_says: Add the volumes of the two parts. Take care to use the right sides.
A cube has three equal sides. If two identical cubes total 128, each is 64.
For layers of liquid, use the base area times the thickness of the layer.
Tape diagrams work for three prisms too.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Problem Set figures were stripped. These problems use the numbers in the Problem Set text. Answers are computed.

teaching_flow.title: Other ways to find the total
teacher_says: Sometimes you can find the total by taking away. Imagine a big prism of 360 cubic meters and cut away a part of 36.
A shorter container does not always have a smaller volume.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: To find the total volume of a composite solid, find each prism's volume. Then add.
Use matching sides or subtraction for missing sides.

explanations.title: Composite solids
explanations.text: A composite solid is made of two prisms joined together. Find the volume of each prism. Then add the volumes.

explanations.title: Finding a missing side
explanations.text: Look for sides that line up in the picture. Or subtract the part you know from the whole length.

explanations.title: Tape diagram for volumes
explanations.text: Draw one bar for each prism. Show how many units each has. Divide the total by the number of units.

explanations.title: Arranging does not change volume
explanations.text: Join the same two prisms a new way. The total volume stays the same.

explanations.title: Subtract a missing part
explanations.text: A solid can be a big prism with a part cut away. Find the big volume. Take away the part.

examples.title: Two boxes: 120 and 30
examples.text: The bottom box is 120 cubic inches. The top box is 30 cubic inches. The total is 150 cubic inches.

examples.title: Finding the top box
examples.text: The bottom edge is 6 m and 4 m sticks out. So the top length is 6 take away 4, which is 2 m. The top box is 2 by 2 by 2, so 8 cubic meters. The bottom is 24. The total is 32 cubic meters.

examples.title: Tape diagram of 135
examples.text: B is 1 unit. A is 2 units. Three units make 135. One unit is 45. A is 90 cubic meters. B is 45 cubic meters.

questions.text: A prism is 3 cm by 4 cm by 2 cm. What is its volume?
A prism has volume 40 cubic inches. It is 4 inches long and 5 inches wide. What is its height?
Partner A builds a structure 3 cm by 2 cm by 2 cm. What is its volume?
Partner B builds a cube that is 2 cm on every side. What is its volume?
We join the two structures into one solid. What is the total volume?
We join them a different way, like an L shape. Does the total volume change?
Why does the volume stay the same?
A prism is 3 m by 2 m by 7 m. What is its volume?
We glue an identical prism to it. What is the total volume?
The bottom box of a solid has a volume of 120 cubic inches. The top box has 30. What is the total volume?
The top box has no width shown. It lines up with the bottom box, which is 5 inches wide. What is the top box's width?
In another solid, the whole bottom edge is 6 m. The top box sticks out 4 m. What is the length of the other part?
The top box is 2 m long, 2 m wide and 4 m high. What is its volume?
The bottom box is 6 m by 2 m by 2 m. What is its volume?
What is the total volume of both prisms in this solid?
Two prisms have a combined volume of 135 cubic meters. Prism A has double the volume of Prism B. How many units are in the tape diagram?
One unit is 135 divided by 3. What is the volume of Prism B?
What is the volume of Prism A?
One face of Prism A has an area of 10 square meters. What is its height?
A cube storage unit has a volume of 64 cubic meters. What is each edge?
The Double storage unit has twice the volume of the Cube. What is its volume?
The Half storage unit has half the volume of the Cube. What is its volume?
A sculpture has two prisms. The first is 13 in by 8 in by 2 in. What is its volume?
The second prism is 9 in by 8 in by 18 in. What is its volume?
What is the total volume of the whole sculpture?
Two identical cubes have a combined volume of 128 cubic centimeters. What is the volume of one cube?
What is the side length of one of those cubes?
A tank has a base area of 24 square cm. Water and oil fill it to 9 cm deep. The oil layer is 4 cm thick. How thick is the water layer?
What is the volume of the water in that tank?
Three prisms have a combined volume of 518 cubic feet. B and C are equal. A is one third of B. How many units in all?
What is the volume of Prism A, the smallest prism? Each unit is 518 divided by 7.
What is the volume of Prism B?
A friend cannot see the missing sides on a composite solid. What can you tell them?
Imagine a solid made of a big prism of 360 cubic meters. A part of 36 cubic meters is cut away. What is the volume left?
Is a shorter container always a smaller volume?
Give an example of a shorter container that holds more.

hints.text: Find the volume of each part first. Then put the two parts together.
A missing side can match another side on the picture. Look for sides that line up.
A missing length can be the whole length take away the part you know.
Add the volumes of the two prisms. That is the total volume.
The tape diagram has parts. Count the equal units. Divide the total by the units.
Find the value of 1 unit first. Then find each prism.

objective.text: Solve word problems about the volume of rectangular prisms with whole number edge lengths.

big_idea.text: Volume is length times width times height. Work backward by dividing. Doubling all three sides makes the volume 8 times as big.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The amount of space inside a solid.
vocabulary.example: A planter with 48 cubic feet of soil.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A unit for volume, such as cubic feet.
The area of the bottom of a box. Length times width.
vocabulary.example: 8 feet times 2 feet is 16 square feet.

vocabulary.kid_definition: Make twice as big.

intro.hook: Geoffrey builds planters and a shed. How much soil does each one hold?
intro.why_it_matters: Builders, gardeners and packers all use volume to pick the right size.
intro.link_to_before: You know the volume formula for a box.
intro.today_goal: Today you solve real problems with it. You also work backward and see what doubling does.

teaching_flow.title: Geoffrey the gardener
teacher_says: Geoffrey builds garden planters. He also wants a new shed.
He needs to know how much soil each planter holds. He also needs the space inside the shed.
Volume answers both.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up: the volume formula
teacher_says: Volume of a box is length times width times height.
Take a box 5 by 6 by 2 centimeters. Its volume is 60 cubic centimeters.
A cube with every edge 4 inches has a volume of 64 cubic inches.
Volume is always in cubic units.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 1: soil in a planter
teacher_says: Plan for any word problem. Can you draw something? What can you draw? What does the drawing tell you?
Geoffrey's first planter is 8 feet long and 2 feet wide. The soil is 3 feet deep.
Draw a box. Label 8, 2 and 3. Find the floor area first, then the volume.
Check at the end. Does the answer make sense?
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is the floor area? What do we multiply it by?

teaching_flow.title: Problem 2: four different planters
teacher_says: Geoffrey wants four tomato planters. Each has a volume of 320 cubic feet. All four must be different.
This is a whole to parts problem. Find three whole numbers that multiply to 320.
Think of 32 tens. 320 is 32 times 10. So factors of 32 help.
Some sets work. Try 10 by 8 by 4. Try 20 by 8 by 2. Try 40 by 4 by 2.
Do not just swap the names length and width. Change the numbers.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what two numbers multiply to 32? Then use a ten.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 3: work backward
teacher_says: Geoffrey wants one planter under a window. The window starts 3 feet off the ground.
The planter must hold 36 cubic feet. It can be at most 3 feet tall.
Volume is floor area times height. So 36 divided by 3 gives a floor area of 12 square feet.
Floors that work: 12 by 1, or 6 by 2, or 4 by 3.
The same floor area can have different shapes.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: volume equals floor area times height. What is missing?

teaching_flow.title: Problem 4: the new shed
teacher_says: The old shed is 6 feet long, 5 feet wide and 8 feet high. Its volume is 240 cubic feet.
Geoffrey needs 480 cubic feet. That is twice as much.
Doubling all three sides makes 12 by 10 by 16. The volume is 1,920 cubic feet. That is 8 times as big. Too big.
Doubling just one side gives 480. Keep height 8. The floor must be 60 square feet.
Other floors work too. Halve the length to 3 and make the width 20.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many sides did we double? Each one doubles the volume.

teaching_flow.title: Wren's boxes
teacher_says: Wren makes display boxes. Her first box is 6 inches by 9 inches by 4 inches.
Her soccer box is 1 foot by 2 feet by 2 feet. She wants 12 cubic feet.
She doubles only the width. Check if that is enough.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Wren's three shadow boxes of 60 cubic inches and the stencil box of 72 cubic inches are other questions in the source. Not made into questions here.

teaching_flow.title: What doubling does
teacher_says: Double one side and the volume doubles. Double two sides and it is 4 times as big. Double three sides and it is 8 times as big.
Double one side and halve another. The volume stays the same.
Jean doubled all three sides. She said the volume only doubles. Was she right?

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Draw, find the floor area, then multiply by the height. To work backward, divide. Doubling each side makes the volume 8 times as big.

explanations.title: Plan for word problems
explanations.text: Ask three things. Can you draw something? What can you draw? What does the drawing tell you? Then calculate, write a sentence and check that the answer makes sense.

explanations.title: Working backward with volume
explanations.text: If you know the volume and the height, divide to find the floor area. If you know the volume and the floor area, divide to find the height. Many floors can have the same area.

explanations.title: Many boxes, one volume
explanations.text: Different boxes can have the same volume. Find three whole numbers that multiply to the volume. Change the numbers, not just the names.

explanations.title: What doubling does to volume
explanations.text: Doubling one side doubles the volume. Doubling two sides makes it 4 times as big. Doubling all three sides makes it 8 times as big. Doubling one side and halving another keeps the volume.

explanations.title: Units for volume
explanations.text: Volume uses cubic units, such as cubic feet. The floor area uses square units, such as square feet. Always write the unit.

examples.title: Geoffrey's first planter
examples.text: The planter is 8 feet long, 2 feet wide, with soil 3 feet deep. The floor is 16 square feet. The volume is 48 cubic feet.

examples.title: Geoffrey's shed
examples.text: Old shed 6 by 5 by 8 is 240 cubic feet. Double all sides to get 12 by 10 by 16. That is 1,920 cubic feet. That is 8 times as big. Double only the length to get 480 cubic feet.

examples.title: Planter under the window
examples.text: Volume is 36 cubic feet and height is 3 feet. The floor is 12 square feet. A floor of 6 by 2 works. So does 4 by 3.

A cube has every edge 4 inches long. What is its volume?

The soil in the planter is 3 feet deep. What is the volume of the soil?
Geoffrey wants a planter with a volume of 320 cubic feet. Is 10 feet by 8 feet by 4 feet right?

To go from volume to floor area, which operation do we use?
A planter floor is 6 feet by 2 feet. It is 3 feet high. What is its volume?
The window starts 3 feet off the ground. Can a planter 3 feet high go under it?
Geoffrey's old shed is 6 feet by 5 feet by 8 feet. What is its volume?
Geoffrey doubles all three sides of the shed. What is the new volume?
How many times as big as the old shed is the new shed? Say the number.
Geoffrey needs 480 cubic feet. Is the shed with all three sides doubled too big?
What is the volume if Geoffrey doubles only the length of the shed?
The height stays 8 feet. What floor area gives a volume of 480 cubic feet?
Geoffrey halves the length to 3 feet. The width must grow to make a floor of 60 square feet. How wide is it?
Wren's display box is 6 inches long, 9 inches wide and 4 inches high. What is its volume?
Wren's box is 1 foot by 2 feet by 2 feet. She doubles the width only. Is the volume 12 cubic feet?
What happens to the volume when you double one side?
What happens to the volume when you double two sides?
What happens to the volume when you double one side and halve another?
Jean's shed is 6 meters by 5 meters by 12 meters. She doubles all three sides. She says the volume only doubles. Is she correct?

hints.text: Volume is length times width times height. Which three numbers do we have?
Volume counts cubes. The unit is cubic feet or cubic inches, not square.
Find the area of the floor first. Then multiply by the height.
Think of three whole numbers that multiply to the volume. Try a factor of the volume first.
We know the volume and one side. Divide the volume by that side to find the rest.
Volume divided by height gives the area of the base.
Write the new sides first. Then multiply all three. Compare with the old volume.
Each doubled side doubles the volume once. How many sides did we double?
Does your answer make sense? Compare it with the number you need.

objective.text: Use volume ideas and formulas to plan a sculpture of rectangular prisms that follows rules.

big_idea.text: Pick sides to get a volume. A half or a third prism changes one side. Add all volumes and stay under the limit.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The amount of space inside a solid.
A solid shaped like a box.
A rule your project must follow.
A checklist for how work is judged.

intro.hook: Imagine a sculpture built only from boxes. Which boxes would you need?
intro.why_it_matters: Designers and builders plan with numbers first. This saves time and material.
intro.link_to_before: You can find the volume of a box. You can work backward to find a side.
intro.today_goal: Today you plan a sculpture that follows rules about its volume.

teaching_flow.title: You are the sculptor
teacher_says: Think of a sculpture made of boxes. Maybe a letter, a tree house or a robot.
Today you plan one. The boxes must follow some rules.
The math tells you which boxes you can use.

teaching_flow.title: The rules
teacher_says: The sculpture has 5 to 7 prisms. Each prism gets a letter, starting with A. Each one shows its sides and its volume.
Prism D must be one half the volume of another prism.
Prism E must be one third the volume of another prism.
The total volume must be 1,000 cubic centimeters or less.
A rubric tells you how your work is judged.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The source rule lines lost the fractions. Half and one third are rebuilt from the teacher's words. Check the original.

teaching_flow.title: Make a box with a chosen volume
teacher_says: The class gets flat box patterns with three different bases. You change the volume by cutting the side flaps to a different height.
Take the base of 6 by 3 centimeters. Its floor area is 18 square centimeters.
We want a volume of 36 cubic centimeters. Divide 36 by 18. The height is 2 centimeters.
Cut the flaps 2 centimeters high. Fold. Tape.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is the floor area? Volume divided by floor area gives the height.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The child does not cut or tape here. Use the picture and talk through the plan.

teaching_flow.title: Plan the half prism
teacher_says: Prism A has a volume of 36. Prism D must be half of that.
Half of 36 is 18. Two plans work. Use the same base and cut the height in half. Or pick new sides that give 18.
Halve only one side. Halve two sides and you get one fourth.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is half of 36? How tall is the box if the base stays the same?

source_ref.section: Concept Development (student ideas for Prism D)

teaching_flow.title: Plan the third prism
teacher_says: Prism E must be one third of another prism. Start with a big prism of 420 cubic centimeters.
One third of 420 is 140. Divide by 3.
You can also cut one side of a prism to one third. A 12 centimeter side becomes 4.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: split 420 into 3 equal parts. How big is one part?

source_ref.section: Concept Development (student ideas for Prism E)

teaching_flow.title: Stay under 1,000
teacher_says: A student plans a prism of 420, one of 210 and one of 140. The total is 770.
That leaves 230 cubic centimeters and two more prisms.
The student adds two more prisms. One is 3 by 6 by 4. One is 5 by 5 by 4. They are 72 and 100. The total is 942.
942 is less than 1,000. The plan works. Always add up the whole plan before you cut.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is the total so far? How much is left under 1,000?

source_ref.section: Concept Development (student ideas for the total)

teaching_flow.title: Problem Set practice
teacher_says: A prism is 6 by 12 by 15 centimeters. Find its volume. Then plan prisms with a fraction of that volume.
Sunni's bedroom is 11 feet by 10 feet by 10 feet. Her den has the same height and double the volume.
Double the volume with the same height means the floor must be double.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Problem 1 asks for a sketch of a 36 cubic centimeter prism with blank dimensions. It is covered by q_pr_2.

teaching_flow.title: How did you plan?
teacher_says: There are two ways to find a half or a third prism. Change one side, or find the new volume first and pick sides.
Think about your design. What was the hardest part?

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Floor area times height gives volume. Volume divided by floor area gives height. Add all prisms and check the limit.

explanations.title: Choosing the height for a volume
explanations.text: Pick a base. Find its area. Divide the volume you want by the area. That is the height to cut. Check by multiplying all three sides.

explanations.title: A half or a third of a prism
explanations.text: To get one half of the volume, halve one side or halve the volume first. For one third, cut one side to one third or divide the volume by 3. Change only one side.

explanations.title: Planning with a volume limit
explanations.text: Add the volumes as you plan. Subtract from the limit to see what is left. The total of all prisms must be 1,000 cubic centimeters or less.

explanations.title: Double the volume, same height
explanations.text: Keep the height. Double the floor area. A floor of 110 square feet becomes 220. Many floors have the same area, such as 22 by 10 or 20 by 11.

examples.title: A plan with five prisms
examples.text: Prisms of 420, 210, 140, 72 and 100 cubic centimeters. Total is 942. This is under 1,000. 210 is half of 420 and 140 is one third of 420.

examples.title: A box with volume 36
examples.text: Base 6 by 3 has area 18. Height 2 gives volume 36. Half height 1 gives 18.

objective.text: Apply volume ideas to review a sculpture of rectangular prisms against its requirements.

big_idea.text: A reviewer checks each rule with numbers. The small prism is the half or third. Add all volumes and compare with 1,000.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A checklist for how work is judged.
A rule the project must meet.
The amount of space inside a solid.
All the volumes added together.

intro.hook: Teachers use a checklist to grade a project. Today you are the grader.
intro.why_it_matters: Checking work with numbers helps you find mistakes in your own work too.
intro.link_to_before: Last time you planned a sculpture with rules.
intro.today_goal: Today you check a sample sculpture against those rules.

teaching_flow.title: Be the judge
teacher_says: Today you are the reviewer. A classmate made a sculpture from boxes.
You check it against a rubric. A rubric is a checklist of rules.
You do not guess. You check each number.

teaching_flow.title: The rules and the student sculpture
teacher_says: Here are the rules from Lesson 8. The sculpture needs 5 to 7 prisms.
Each prism has a letter, its sides and its volume. Prism D is one half of another prism. Prism E is one third of another. The total is 1,000 cubic centimeters or less.
The student sculpture has five prisms, A to E. The volumes written are A 36, B 420, C 36, D 18 and E 140.
The reviewer works anonymously. The project has a number, not a name.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source figure of the student sculpture is a picture and was stripped. Volumes come from the teacher's lines. The sides are generated.

teaching_flow.title: Confirm the volumes first
teacher_says: Before we review, check the recorded numbers. Multiply the sides of each prism.
Do not trust the label. If your volume is different, put a star by the prism label.
Prism B is 7 by 10 by 6. That is 420. Prisms A and C are both 36. Prism D is 18. Prism E is 140.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what are the three sides? Multiply them.

teaching_flow.title: Counts, labels and units
teacher_says: First requirement. How many prisms? Check the box and write the number.
Next. Does each prism have a letter? Are sides and volume on each label?
Then units. Sides are in centimeters. Volume is in cubic centimeters.
The Notes box is for a nice comment or for something missing.

teaching_flow.title: The half and third rules
teacher_says: Prism D is 18. Is it half of another prism? Half of 36 is 18. Yes. Prism D is half of Prism A.
Prism E is 140. Is it one third of another prism? 140 times 3 is 420. Yes. Prism E is one third of Prism B.
The small prism is the half or third. Do not flip them.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: which prism is smaller? Multiply the small volume to get the big one.

teaching_flow.title: The total volume
teacher_says: Add all five volumes. 36 plus 36 plus 18 plus 140 plus 420 is 650.
The limit is 1,000. 650 is less than 1,000. The total rule is met.
The sculpture is 350 under the limit.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what do you get when you add them? Is it more than 1,000?

teaching_flow.title: The verdict
teacher_says: Count what we found. Five prisms. Letters and labels. Correct units. D is half of A. E is one third of B. The total is 650.
Every rule is met. The student passes.
If a rule is not met, write it in the Notes box. Be kind and helpful.

teaching_flow.title: Reviewing and creating
teacher_says: Compare the sculpture you reviewed with a design you could make.
If a design missed a rule, what feedback would you give?
Would you change your own design now?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The source has the child review a real classmate's project. That is not tutorable here, so the child uses the sample sculpture.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Check each rule one by one. Confirm the volumes first. The small prism is the half or the third. Add up and compare with the limit.

explanations.title: How to review a design
explanations.text: Confirm the volumes first. Then go down the rubric one line at a time. Record what you find. Write kind notes. If a number differs, put a star by the prism.

explanations.title: Checking half and one third
explanations.text: Take the small prism. Multiply its volume by 2 to see if it is a half. Multiply it by 3 to see if it is a third. Does the answer match the big prism?

explanations.title: Checking the total
explanations.text: Add the volumes of all prisms. Compare with the limit of 1,000 cubic centimeters. Less than or equal to 1,000 meets the rule.

explanations.title: Units on the labels
explanations.text: Sides are lengths, so they use centimeters. Volume counts cubes, so it uses cubic centimeters. A good label shows both.

examples.title: The student sculpture
examples.text: Five prisms. A 36, B 420, C 36, D 18, E 140 cubic centimeters. D is half of A. E is one third of B. The total is 650.

examples.title: Two checks
examples.text: 18 times 2 is 36, so D is half of A. 140 times 3 is 420, so E is one third of B.

questions.text: A box is 6 centimeters by 3 centimeters by 2 centimeters. What is its volume?
What is half of 36?
What is one third of 420? Say the number.
The student sculpture has prisms A, B, C, D and E. How many prisms is that?
The project needs 5 to 7 prisms. Does this sculpture meet that rule?
Are all the prisms labeled with a letter, their sides and their volume?
What unit do the sides use on the labels?
What unit do the volumes use on the labels?
Before we review, we check the recorded volumes. Prism B has sides 7, 10 and 6 centimeters. What is its volume?
Which two prisms have the same volume of 36 cubic centimeters?
Prism D has a volume of 18 cubic centimeters. It must be one half of another prism. Which prism?
Check it. What is two times 18?
Prism E has a volume of 140 cubic centimeters. It must be one third of another prism. Which prism?
Check it. What is 3 times 140?
What is the total volume of the sculpture? The volumes are 36, 36, 18, 140 and 420.
The limit is 1,000 cubic centimeters. Is 650 within the limit?
How many cubic centimeters is the sculpture under the limit?
A sculpture has a total volume of 1,050 cubic centimeters. Does it meet the rules?
A reviewer measures a prism and gets a different volume than the label. What should the reviewer do?
Where do you write a nice comment, or a missing part of the design?
Did this student meet all the requirements?
How do you know the student met every requirement? Name the rules you checked.
How is reviewing a design different from creating one?

objective.text: Find the area of rectangles with fraction sides by tiling and by multiplying.

big_idea.text: Cover a rectangle with whole tiles and part tiles. Or split the side, find each part and add.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The number of square units that cover a flat shape.
A square with sides of 1 unit.
Break a number into parts.
vocabulary.example: 2 and 1 half is 2 plus one half.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The area of one part of a split rectangle.

intro.hook: A floor ends in the middle of a tile. How do you cover it? You cut a tile.
intro.why_it_matters: Builders and designers cover spaces with part tiles. They count the area.
intro.link_to_before: You know area of a rectangle with whole sides.
intro.today_goal: Today the sides have halves. You find the area by tiling and by multiplying.

teaching_flow.title: Covering a floor
teacher_says: Think about tiles on a floor. You cover the floor with square tiles. You count the tiles.
What if the floor ends in the middle of a tile? You cut a tile.
Today we cover rectangles with whole tiles and part tiles.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up and the first rectangle
teacher_says: Area is measured in square units. One tile is one square unit.
Rectangle A is 3 units long and 2 units wide. We cover it with 6 tiles. The area is 6 square units.
We do not need to draw every tile. Label the length and the width. We can imagine the tiles.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many tiles in one row? How many rows?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The source has the child tile with patty paper and sketch. Not tutorable. Use the picture.

teaching_flow.title: Rectangle B: a part tile
teacher_says: Rectangle B is as long as A, but wider. Its area is greater than A.
It is wider than 2 tiles but not as wide as 3. We fold a tile to fill the gap.
The fold makes two equal parts. So we need half tiles. We use 3 half tiles across the length.
The width of B is 2 and 1 half units.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: does the extra part fill a whole tile? How many equal parts does the fold make?

teaching_flow.title: Rectangle B: count the tiles
teacher_says: Count the whole tiles first. There are 6. Then add the halves. There are 3 halves.
Two halves make 1 whole. So 3 halves is 1 and 1 half.
6 plus 1 and 1 half is 7 and 1 half. The area of B is 7 and 1 half square units.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many wholes? How many halves? What do the halves make?

teaching_flow.title: Rectangle B: split and multiply
teacher_says: Split the width. 2 and 1 half is 2 plus one half. Draw a line across the rectangle.
The top part is 3 by 2. Its area is 6 square units.
The bottom part is 3 by one half. 3 copies of one half is 3 halves. That is 1 and 1 half square units.
Add the parts. The area is 7 and 1 half square units. It matches the tiles.
It makes sense. B is only a little wider than A.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: which part is 3 by 2? Which part is 3 by one half?

teaching_flow.title: Rectangles C, D and E
teacher_says: Rectangle E is one half unit wide and 5 units long. 5 halves make 2 and 1 half square units.
Rectangle C is 2 and 1 half wide and 5 long. Split it into 2 by 5, and one half by 5.
Rectangle D is 2 long and 1 and 1 half wide. Split it into 2 by 1, and 2 by one half.
Notice C is 5 times as big as E.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what are the whole parts? What is the fraction part? Add the two areas.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The side lengths of C, D and E were lost. These are generated stand-ins. See flags.

teaching_flow.title: Soil and perimeter problems
teacher_says: Heidi's flowerbed is 5 feet by 3 feet. Andrew's is the same length but twice as wide. Soil is 2 feet deep. Find the soil for both beds.
Now a perimeter problem. A rectangle has a perimeter of 27 feet. The length is 12 feet. Find the width, then the area.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Perimeter value was lost in the source. 27 is a stand-in.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Cover a rectangle with whole tiles and part tiles. Or split the side and multiply. Add the parts. The area is in square units.

explanations.title: Tiling with part tiles
explanations.text: Cover the rectangle with whole tiles. Fold a tile to fit any gap. A fold into two equal parts makes halves. Count whole tiles, then add the parts.

explanations.title: Split the side and multiply
explanations.text: Split a mixed number into a whole number and a fraction. Find the area of each part. Then add. Three times 2 and 1 half is 3 times 2, plus 3 times one half.

explanations.title: A whole number times a half
explanations.text: 3 times one half means 3 copies of one half. That is 3 halves. Two halves make one whole. So 3 halves is 1 and 1 half.

explanations.title: Does the area make sense?
explanations.text: Compare with a rectangle you know. B is only a little wider than A. So its area is only a little more than 6.

examples.title: Rectangle B
examples.text: 3 units long. 2 and 1 half units wide. 6 whole tiles and 3 half tiles. The area is 7 and 1 half square units.

examples.title: Rectangle C (stand-in)
examples.text: 2 and 1 half units wide and 5 long. The whole part gives 10 square units. The half part gives 2 and 1 half.

questions.text: A rectangle is 4 units long and 3 units wide. What is its area?
How many halves make 1 whole?
What is 3 halves as a mixed number?
What kind of units do we use to measure area?
Rectangle A is 3 units long and 2 units wide. We cover it with whole tiles. What is its area?
If we only label the length and the width, can we still know the area?
Rectangle B is as long as A but wider. Is its area greater than or less than the area of A?
Rectangle B is wider than 2 tiles but not as wide as 3 tiles. What fraction of a tile covers the extra width?
What is the width of Rectangle B? Say it in units.
Count the whole tiles first, then the halves. What is the area of Rectangle B?
We split 2 and 1 half into 2 plus a part. What is the part?
The first part is 3 units long and 2 units wide. What is its area?
The second part is 3 units long and one half unit wide. What is its area?
Add the two parts. 6 plus 1 and 1 half. Does 7 and 1 half make sense for Rectangle B?
Rectangle E is one half unit wide and 5 units long. What is its area?
Rectangle C is 2 and 1 half units wide and 5 units long. What is its area?
C is 2 and 1 half units wide. E is one half unit wide. Both are 5 units long. How many times as big is the area of C as E?
Rectangle D is 2 units long and 1 and 1 half units wide. What is its area?
Heidi's flowerbed is 5 feet by 3 feet. Andrew's is the same length but twice as wide. Both are filled 2 feet deep. How many cubic feet of soil in all?
A rectangle has a perimeter of 27 feet. The length is 12 feet. How wide is it?
What is the area of that rectangle?
When we record tiling, must we sketch every tile?
We have the area of each part. What do we do to get the total?
How did you find the area of Rectangle E? Did you count, add again and again, or multiply the sides?

objective.text: Find the area of rectangles with fraction sides on both sides by tiling and multiplying.

big_idea.text: Split both sides into whole and fraction parts. A rectangle then has 4 parts. Multiply each part and add.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The number of square units that cover a flat shape.
The area of one part of a split rectangle.
vocabulary.example: One half by one half is one fourth.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A whole number and a fraction together.
One of 4 equal parts. Half of a half.

intro.hook: A board is 6 and 1 half feet by 4 feet. How many squares cover it?
intro.why_it_matters: People who tile floors or walls find the area with part tiles all the time.
intro.link_to_before: Last time you found area when one side had a fraction.
intro.today_goal: Today both sides have fractions. You will tile, then multiply, and check that they match.

teaching_flow.title: Covering a bulletin board
teacher_says: Mrs. Golden has a bulletin board that is 6 and 1 half feet by 4 feet. She covers it with silver paper squares. Each square is 1 foot wide.
Does the paper fit with no cutting? It needs a half column.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many whole columns? What is left over? How many halves fit in it?

teaching_flow.title: Last time and today
teacher_says: Last time one side had a fraction. Today both sides can have fractions.
We tile a rectangle with whole tiles, then half tiles, then an even smaller tile.
We also record the parts and multiply to check.

teaching_flow.title: Rectangle A: the whole tiles
teacher_says: Rectangle A is 4 and 1 half units long. It is 2 and 1 half units wide.
Start at the top left corner. Place whole tiles. 8 whole tiles fit.
This is not the area yet. There is more to cover.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many tiles in one row? How many rows?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The child does not tile with paper. Use the picture and the teacher's counts. Sides of A are rebuilt from those counts.

teaching_flow.title: Rectangle A: halves and the corner
teacher_says: Fold tiles to cover the rest of the length. We need 2 half tiles.
Fold tiles to cover the rest of the width. We need 4 half tiles.
One small part is left in the corner. It is half of a half. That is one fourth of a square unit.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: does a half tile fit the corner? What happens if we fold the half again?

teaching_flow.title: Rectangle A: count the area
teacher_says: Count the whole tiles. 8 squares. Then 6 halves. 6 halves make 3 squares. That is 11.
Add the one fourth. The area is 11 and 1 fourth square units.
Another way. 2 rows of 4 and 1 half make 9. Then 4 halves and one fourth. 9 plus 2 and 1 fourth is 11 and 1 fourth.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what do 6 halves make? Add the corner.

teaching_flow.title: Rectangle A: split and multiply
teacher_says: Split the length as 4 plus one half. Split the width as 2 plus one half.
There are 4 parts. Whole by whole. Whole by half. Half by whole. Half by half.
2 by 4 is 8. 2 by one half is 1. One half by 4 is 2. One half by one half is one fourth.
Add them. 8 plus 1 plus 2 plus one fourth is 11 and 1 fourth. It matches the tiles.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: which part is whole by whole? Which is half by half?

teaching_flow.title: Other rectangles
teacher_says: Try the same steps on new rectangles. Split each side. Find four parts. Add.
Rectangle B is 3 and 1 half by 1 and 1 half. Rectangle C is one half by 2 and 1 half. Rectangle D is one half by one half.
Think about D. A part of a part is smaller than either part.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what are the four parts? What is each one? Add.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The sides of B, C, D and E were lost. Stand-ins are used and flagged.

teaching_flow.title: A square from its perimeter
teacher_says: A square has a perimeter of 25 inches. A square has 4 equal sides.
Divide 25 by 4 to get the side. Then find the area by multiplying the side by itself.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many equal sides? What is 25 divided by 4?

teaching_flow.title: Compare with yesterday
teacher_says: Yesterday only one side had a fraction. Today both do.
When both sides have a part, we get 4 partial products.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Cover with whole tiles, then halves, then a smaller tile. Or split both sides into four parts. Multiply each part and add.

explanations.title: Four parts when both sides have fractions
explanations.text: Split each side into a whole number and a fraction. The rectangle breaks into 4 parts. Find the area of each part. Add all four.

explanations.title: Half of a half
explanations.text: Fold a half tile in half again. You get 2 equal parts. Each part is one fourth of a whole tile. So one half of one half is one fourth.

explanations.title: Turn halves into wholes
explanations.text: Two halves make 1 whole. So 4 halves make 2 wholes. 6 halves make 3 wholes. Do this before you add.

explanations.title: Tiling and multiplying agree
explanations.text: The area from counting tiles and the area from multiplying must match. If not, look for a missing part or a half counted as a whole.
