objective.text: Measure to find the area of rectangles with fractional side lengths.

big_idea.text: Split each side into whole and fraction parts. Find each small area. Add them.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The flat space inside a shape. We count square units.
vocabulary.example: A 4 by 3 rectangle has an area of 12 square units.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The area of one small part of a split rectangle.
vocabulary.example: The 2 by one half part has an area of 1 square inch.

vocabulary.kid_definition: To break a side into whole units and a fraction.
vocabulary.example: 2 and one half splits into 2 and one half.

vocabulary.kid_definition: Parts must use the same fraction unit before we add.

intro.hook: How much paper does a jar label need? The sides are not whole numbers.
intro.why_it_matters: People find area of rooms, gardens and paper. Sides are often not whole numbers.
intro.link_to_before: You found areas by tiling and multiplying in Lessons 10 and 11.
intro.today_goal: Today you measure and find the area of rectangles with fraction sides.

teaching_flow.title: A label for a jar
teacher_says: Imagine you design a label for a jar. The sides are not whole numbers.
How much paper do you need? Today we find the area of rectangles with side lengths that have fractions.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up
teacher_says: Area is the flat space inside a shape. We count square units.
A rectangle 4 inches by 3 inches has an area of 12 square inches.
We also need fraction times a whole number and fraction times fraction.

teaching_flow.title: Measure and estimate
teacher_says: Today we use a ruler. We measure the sides. Then we multiply the side lengths.
The first rectangle is 2 inches by 2 and one half inches.
First, estimate. A 2 inch square has an area of 4 square inches. Our rectangle is a little longer.
The long side is between 2 and 3 inches. So the area is between 4 and 6 square inches.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what if both sides were 2? What if both sides were 3?

teaching_flow.title: Split the rectangle in parts
teacher_says: Split the long side into 2 whole inches and one half inch. Draw a line there.
Now we have two parts. One part is 2 inches by 2 inches. The other part is 2 inches by one half inch.
The first part is 4 square inches. The second part is 1 square inch, because 2 halves make 1.
Add the parts. Four and one make 5 square inches. It is between 4 and 6, so it makes sense.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many tiles go across? How many rows? Then what is two times one half?

teaching_flow.title: A square with fraction sides
teacher_says: The next rectangle is a square. Each side is 1 and three fourths inches.
Estimate first. The sides are almost 2 inches. So the area is a little less than 4 square inches.
Split each side into 1 and three fourths. Now the square has four parts.
The 1 by 1 part is 1 square inch. Two parts are 1 by three fourths. Each is three fourths of a square inch.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many pieces are on each side? Four parts in all.

teaching_flow.title: The corner and the total
teacher_says: The last part is a little square. Each side is three fourths of an inch.
It is smaller than the other parts. Both sides are less than one inch.
Multiply the sides. Three fourths times three fourths is nine sixteenths.
To add, use the same unit. Change every part to sixteenths. Then add all four parts.
The total area is 49 sixteenths, or 3 and one sixteenth square inches.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is three times three? What is four times four?

teaching_flow.title: Try it on real problems
teacher_says: Now use the area model on your own. A label is 2 and one half inches by 1 and one half inches.
Then try rooms and paper. Find each part. Add the parts. Take away parts that are cut out.
Check the answer. Does it make sense?
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Draw four boxes. Find each small area. Then add.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The problem set uses ruler measuring on paper. That is not tutorable. All problems here use numbers given in words.

teaching_flow.title: Look back
teacher_says: A half of a fraction is easy to find. Double the bottom number.
Look at what stays the same. One side gets 5 times longer. The other gets one fifth as wide. The area stays the same.
In a square, the two middle parts match, because the sides match.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: We split each side into whole and fraction parts. We find the area of each small part. Then we add the parts. Check with an estimate.

explanations.title: Estimate before you multiply
explanations.text: Look at the whole numbers on each side. A side of 2 and one half is between 2 and 3. So the area is between 2 times and 3 times the other side. Check your answer against this.

explanations.title: Split each side into parts
explanations.text: Split each long side into whole units and a fraction. Draw a line for each split. Each pair of pieces makes a small rectangle. Find the area of each small rectangle. Then add.

explanations.title: A fraction times a fraction
explanations.text: To multiply two fractions, multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms. Three fourths times three fourths is nine sixteenths. The answer is smaller than each factor, because both are less than one.

explanations.title: Add with the same unit
explanations.text: We can only add parts that use the same unit. Change one whole, three fourths and nine sixteenths into sixteenths. Then add the tops.

explanations.title: Use a ruler for side lengths
explanations.text: A ruler measures the sides. It does not show square units. Measure the sides, then multiply the side lengths to get the area. The answer is in square units.

examples.title: 2 inches by 2 and one half inches
examples.text: Split the long side into 2 and one half. The 2 by 2 part is 4 square inches. The 2 by one half part is 1 square inch. Total area is 5 square inches.

examples.title: A square 1 and three fourths inches on a side
examples.text: Four parts: 1 by 1 is 1. Two parts of 1 by three fourths are three fourths each. The corner is nine sixteenths. Total is 3 and one sixteenth square inches.

questions.text: A rectangle is 4 inches by 3 inches. What is its area?
What is 2 times one half? Say it as a whole number.
What is 3 fourths times 1?
A rectangle is 2 inches wide. Its long side is 2 and one half inches. If it were a 2 inch square, what would the area be?
The long side is a little more than 2 inches. It is less than 3 inches. Between which two whole numbers is the area?
We split the long side into 2 whole inches and one half inch. What is the area of the 2 inch by 2 inch part?
Now find the area of the smaller part. It is 2 inches by one half inch. What is its area?
What is the total area of the rectangle?
Does 5 square inches make sense? Our estimate was between 4 and 6.
A square has sides of 1 and three fourths inches. Will its area be less than 4 square inches?
We split each side into 1 and three fourths. How many small parts does the square have?
Two parts are 1 inch by three fourths inch. What is the area of each one?
The last corner part is three fourths inch by three fourths inch. Is its area greater or less than the other parts?
What is the area of the corner part, three fourths inch by three fourths inch?
We have 16 sixteenths in 1 whole. How many sixteenths are in three fourths?
Add the four parts in sixteenths: 16, 12, 12 and 9. What is the total area of the square?
A label is 2 and one half inches by 1 and one half inches. The parts are 2, 1, one half and one fourth. What is the area?
A living room is 15 feet by 12 and one half feet. A dining room is 10 feet by 11 and one half feet. How many square feet of carpet cover both rooms?
A rectangle is 4 inches by 3 and one half inches. Fred cuts out a square, 1 and one half inches on a side. How much paper is left?
Kelly's tent is 4 feet wide and has an area of 31 square feet. Her tarp is 8 feet by 4 and one half feet. That is 36 square feet. Can the tarp cover the tent floor?
What is one half times one fourth? Use the trick: double the denominator.
One rectangle is 5 times as long as another. It is one fifth as wide. Does the area change?
In the area model of a square, two parts are always the same. Why?
How can a ruler help you find an area?

hints.text: Think of a square with the shorter side on all sides. Then ask how much longer the real side is.
Picture whole square tiles in the rectangle. Count how many go across and how many rows.
Two times one half means two halves. Two halves make one whole.
Break each long side into ones and a fraction. Each pair of pieces makes one small rectangle.
A whole tile will not fit. We would fold it. The part is less than one square.
Multiply the top fraction by the side fraction. Multiply the numbers on top, then the numbers on the bottom.
To add parts we need the same unit. Change every part to sixteenths first.
Area is measured in square units. Say square inches, not inches.
Compare the side lengths. The shorter sides make the smaller piece.
Find each small area first. Then add all the parts together.
One half of a fraction cuts the pieces in two. The pieces get twice as small.

misconceptions.label: Multiplies only the whole numbers
misconceptions.description: Child finds only the ones by ones part and forgets the fraction parts. Area comes out too small.
detection_signals: child says the area is 4 for the 2 by 2 and one half rectangle
child ignores the fraction of an inch
misconceptions.response_text: The fraction part is real space too. Check the estimate. The area must be between 4 and 6. Add the part from the half inch.

misconceptions.label: Forgets the two middle parts in a square
misconceptions.description: In the square with sides 1 and three fourths, child adds only 1 and nine sixteenths. The two middle rectangles are missed.
detection_signals: child says the total is 1 and nine sixteenths
child counts only two parts
misconceptions.response_text: A square with each side split in two makes four parts, not two. Count the four parts. Two of them are one by three fourths.

misconceptions.label: Adds the denominators when multiplying fractions
misconceptions.description: Child says three fourths times three fourths is nine eighths, or six fourths. Child adds the bottom numbers.
detection_signals: child says nine eighths
child says six fourths
child says the answer is bigger than one
misconceptions.response_text: Multiply the top numbers. Multiply the bottom numbers too. Four times four is sixteen. A part of a part is smaller than each part.

misconceptions.label: Gives area in inches, not square inches
misconceptions.description: Child gives the area as inches. Inches measure length. Area needs square units.
detection_signals: child says 5 inches
child leaves off the word square
misconceptions.response_text: Area counts squares. So the unit is square inches. Length uses inches. Area uses square inches.

misconceptions.label: Thinks a fraction of a fraction is bigger
misconceptions.description: Child thinks the small corner piece should be large because the numbers three and three are big.
detection_signals: child says the corner piece is the biggest
child ignores that both sides are less than one
misconceptions.response_text: Both sides are less than one inch. So the piece is smaller than one square inch. It is smaller than the other parts.

objective.text: Multiply mixed number factors, and relate to the distributive property and the area model.

big_idea.text: You can multiply mixed numbers two ways. Pick the way that fits the numbers.

vocabulary.kid_definition: Multiply each part of a number and then add the results.
vocabulary.example: Split a side into a whole and a fraction, then add the parts.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A fraction that is one or more. The top is bigger than or equal to the bottom.
A whole number and a fraction together.
The area of one small part of the area model.
vocabulary.example: One third times three fourths is one fourth.

intro.hook: A mat around a picture can hide a puzzle. How much can you see?
intro.why_it_matters: Real jobs need area with mixed numbers. Floors, mats and fabric all use it.
intro.link_to_before: In Lesson 12 you found area by splitting sides into parts.
intro.today_goal: Today you compare two ways to multiply mixed numbers. You choose the quicker way.

teaching_flow.title: Which way is quicker?
teacher_says: You can cross a river on a bridge or in a boat. Both get you there.
Today we find areas two ways. Then we choose the quicker way.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up
teacher_says: Remember how to multiply fractions. Multiply the tops, then the bottoms. Cancel when you can.
Also remember that area of a rectangle is length times width.

teaching_flow.title: Method one: area model
teacher_says: The rectangle is 1 and one third inches by 3 and three fourths inches. The sides are given. No need to tile or measure.
Split each side. One side is 1 and one third. The other is 3 and three fourths.
A mixed number is like a two digit number. It has big units and small units.
Add the partial products. That uses the distributive property.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what are the four small rectangles? Name each pair of sides.

teaching_flow.title: Method two: improper fractions
teacher_says: Now use a single unit for each side. Write each side as a fraction greater than one.
1 and one third is 4 thirds. 3 and three fourths is 15 fourths.
Multiply across. The 4 on top and the 4 on the bottom cancel. The 3 goes into 15.
The area is 5 square inches. It is the same as before.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many thirds in one whole? Then add the one third.

teaching_flow.title: A harder pair
teacher_says: Now try 8 and one fourth by 4 and one fourth. Which method will be easier? Predict first.
Improper fractions give 33 fourths by 17 fourths. There are no common factors. The numbers are big.
The area model gives easy parts. 8 times 4 is 32. 8 times one fourth is 2. One fourth times 4 is 1. One fourth times one fourth is one sixteenth.
Both give the same area. Here the area model was easier.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: can you cancel any numbers? If not, try the area model.

teaching_flow.title: Choose a method
teacher_says: Small numbers that cancel suit improper fractions. Big mixed numbers with easy parts suit the area model.
You can start with one method and switch if it gets hard.
A square has sides of 3 and one half meters. Try it.

teaching_flow.title: The picture and the mat
teacher_says: An 8 inch by 10 inch picture rests on a mat. Three fourths of an inch of the mat shows on every side.
We want the area of the mat that you can see. Think of the whole mat without the picture.
Add the border to each side. Find the area of the whole mat. Take away the picture.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many borders are on one side length? Two. One on each end.

teaching_flow.title: A bathroom floor
teacher_says: A bathroom floor is tiled with 12 inch squares. Each tile is one square foot.
Find the floor area. Then use the price for each square foot.

teaching_flow.title: Look back
teacher_says: We used two methods. Both give the same area.
When we add partial products, we use the distributive property.
Mixed numbers are like multi digit numbers. They have big units and small units.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Area model: split, multiply parts, add. Improper fractions: change, multiply, cancel. Choose the quicker way for the numbers you have.

explanations.title: Area model with the distributive property
explanations.text: Split each mixed number into a whole and a fraction. Multiply each part of one side by each part of the other. Add the four partial products. This is the distributive property.

explanations.title: Multiply improper fractions
explanations.text: Write each mixed number as a fraction greater than one. Multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms. Cancel first when numbers match. Change the answer back to a mixed number if you like.

explanations.title: Choose the quicker method
explanations.text: If the numbers are small and cancel, improper fractions are fast. If the numbers are big and parts are easy, the area model is fast. Both give the same area. You can switch if one gets hard.

explanations.title: Find the part that you can see
explanations.text: Add the border to both ends of each side to get the whole mat. Find the whole mat area. Find the picture area. Take away the picture from the whole mat.

explanations.title: Mixed numbers are like two digit numbers
explanations.text: A two digit number has tens and ones. A mixed number has ones and fractions. Both have a big unit and a small unit. So the area model works for both.

examples.title: 1 and one third by 3 and three fourths
examples.text: Area model: 3, three fourths, 1, and one fourth. Add to get 5. Improper fractions: 4 thirds times 15 fourths is 5. Both give 5 square inches.

examples.title: 8 and one fourth by 4 and one fourth
examples.text: Improper fractions give 561 sixteenths. That is hard to change back. The area model gives 32, 2, 1 and one sixteenth. The area is 35 and one sixteenth square inches.

examples.title: Picture on a mat
examples.text: Mat is 9 and one half by 11 and one half. Area is 109 and one fourth. Picture is 80. Visible mat is 29 and one fourth square inches.

misconceptions.label: Changes a mixed number to an improper fraction wrongly

child says 11 thirds
child adds the whole number to the top

misconceptions.label: Believes one method is best every time

objective.text: Solve real-world area problems with fractional side lengths using visual models or equations.

big_idea.text: Draw a model, find each area, add or take away, then check.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A drawing that shows a whole and its parts.
vocabulary.example: A wall is the whole. Windows are a part.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The edge where two pieces of cloth are sewn.
vocabulary.example: A seam uses up a bit of fabric.

intro.hook: Painters, carpet fitters and quilt makers all need area.
intro.why_it_matters: Real jobs have more than one shape. You must add and take away areas.
intro.link_to_before: You can find area with mixed numbers two ways.
intro.today_goal: Today you solve real problems and check each answer.

teaching_flow.title: Paint, tiles and carpet
teacher_says: Walls need paint. Floors need carpet. Quilts need fabric.
Today we solve real problems about area. The side lengths have fractions.

teaching_flow.title: A plan for every problem
teacher_says: Use three steps. Model the problem. Calculate and write a statement. Check if the answer makes sense.
To model, ask: can I draw something? A picture, a tape diagram or an area model can help.
You can use the distributive property or improper fractions. Choose the quicker way.

source_ref.section: Concept Development, Delivery of Instruction; Fluency Practice

teaching_flow.title: Problem 1: a wall with windows
teacher_says: George paints a wall that has two windows. Both windows are the same size.
There are three areas to track. The whole wall. The two windows. The wall that needs paint.
A part whole tape diagram can help. The wall is the whole. The windows are one part. The paint area is the other part.
Find the whole wall, then take away both windows.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is the wall area? What is one window? How many windows?

teaching_flow.title: Problem 2: tiles and half tiles
teacher_says: Joe makes a figure with square tiles. Some tiles are cut in half.
Do not just multiply sides. Think about what area means. Put halves together to make whole tiles.
6 halves make 3 whole tiles. Find the area of one tile. Then find the total.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many halves make one whole tile?

teaching_flow.title: Problem 3: carpet in three rooms
teacher_says: A company carpets three rooms. Keep the three areas in order.
One room size is not given. You must find it from the other sizes.
Add the three areas to find the total carpet.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is the total width? Which widths are given?

teaching_flow.title: Problem 4: sod for a lawn
teacher_says: Mr. Johnson buys sod for his front lawn. These sides are larger than before.
A lot of numbers help here. The distributive property makes it easier.
Sod is sold in whole square feet. The area is close to 1,656, but the lawn is a bit more.
Think: is it worth the extra money for the small part left? What could he do with the 8 ninths of a square foot left over?
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is 18 times 90? Then add the fraction parts.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 5: a class quilt
teacher_says: 24 students each make a quilt square. Each square is 8 inches on each side.
When sewn, every edge loses one fourth inch. A side has two edges. So each side loses one half inch.
Each block is 7 and one half inches on a side. Then find the area and perimeter.
Many layouts work. Moving blocks changes the perimeter. It does not change the area.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many edges does one side have? How much does each lose?

teaching_flow.title: Look back
teacher_says: Which method did you pick? Why? What advice would you give a friend who is stuck?
Always check if the answer makes sense.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Draw a model. Find each area. Add or take away. Check the answer.

explanations.title: Whole minus part
explanations.text: To find a space that needs paint, find the whole wall. Then take away the parts that do not need paint. A tape diagram shows the whole and the parts.

explanations.title: Halves make wholes
explanations.text: Area is the amount of flat space. Two half tiles cover the same space as one whole tile. Put halves together in your mind to count whole tiles.

explanations.title: Sold in whole units
explanations.text: A store may sell sod only in whole square feet. We must buy enough to cover the whole lawn. So we round up, not down. Some sod will be left over.

explanations.title: Seams use up fabric
explanations.text: Sewing blocks together uses up some edge. Each edge loses a small amount. A side has two edges. So each side loses twice that amount.

explanations.title: Layout changes perimeter, not area
explanations.text: The same blocks cover the same area in any layout. Long thin layouts have a longer perimeter. Square layouts have a shorter perimeter.

examples.title: Wall with two windows
examples.text: The wall is 102 square feet. Each window is 8 and three fourths. Two windows are 17 and one half. Paint covers 84 and one half square feet.

examples.title: Class quilt
examples.text: Each block is 8 minus one half, so 7 and one half inches. One block is 56 and one fourth square inches. 24 blocks make 1,350 square inches.

questions.text: What is 1 and one half times 4?
A rectangle is 3 feet by 2 feet. What is its area?
A wall is 12 feet by 8 and one half feet. What is the area of the whole wall?
Each window is 3 and one half feet by 2 and one half feet. What is the area of one window?
There are two windows. How many square feet of the wall does the paint need to cover?
Joe makes a figure with whole tiles and half tiles. It has 6 half tiles. How many whole tiles are they worth?
Each square tile has sides of 2 and one half inches. What is the area of one whole tile?
The figure has 3 whole tiles of area. Each is 6 and one fourth square inches. What is the total area of the figure?
Room A is 8 and one half feet by 6 and one half feet. What is its carpet area?
The three rooms together are 20 feet wide. Room A is 8 and one half feet wide. Room B is 7 and one half feet wide. How wide is Room C?
Room A is 55 and one fourth square feet. Room B is 48 and three fourths. Room C is 26. How many square feet of carpet are needed for all three?
A lawn is 18 and one third feet by 90 and one third feet. What is its area?
Sod is sold only in whole square feet. How many square feet must Mr. Johnson buy to cover the lawn?
Sod costs 19 cents for each square foot. How many dollars will 1,657 square feet cost?
Each quilt square is 8 inches on a side. Every edge loses one fourth inch when sewn. How long is one side of a sewn block?
One sewn block is 7 and one half inches on each side. There are 24 blocks. What is the area of the quilt?
Make a quilt 4 blocks by 6 blocks. Each block is 7 and one half inches. What is the perimeter in inches?
Make the quilt 3 blocks by 8 blocks. Its perimeter is longer. Does its area change?
Which method did you use more, the distributive property or improper fractions? How did you decide?
How do you check that an area answer makes sense?

objective.text: Solve real-world area problems with fractional side lengths using visual models or equations.

big_idea.text: Draw a model, use one unit, find each part, and check the answer.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The distance around a shape.
vocabulary.example: A square with sides of 6 feet has a perimeter of 24 feet.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A square that is 1 yard on each side. It is 9 square feet.
To go all the way around something.
To write a size in a different unit.

intro.hook: A fence around a garden, curtains and wire shapes all need careful math.
intro.why_it_matters: Real problems mix units and many steps. A plan keeps you on track.
intro.link_to_before: Yesterday you solved real area problems with a model and a check.
intro.today_goal: Today you do four harder problems.

teaching_flow.title: Gardens, fabric and wire
teacher_says: Gardens, curtains and wire frames all use area and perimeter.
Today the sides have fractions and different units. We take it one step at a time.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up
teacher_says: Remember: how many halves are in 3? There are 6.
Also remember: a square is a rhombus with right angles. So a square is a rhombus.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 1: a narrow flowerbed
teacher_says: A flowerbed is 4 times as long as it is wide. The width is one third meter.
The length is not given. First find it. Then find the area.
Check the answer. Picture 1 meter square tiles. The bed is longer than 1 meter, so it needs 2 tiles.
The area is less than one square meter. It is a part of a part.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is 4 times one third? Then what is that times one third?

teaching_flow.title: Problem 2: the basil plot
teacher_says: Mrs. Johnson has a square basil plot. Each side is three fourths yard.
First find the area in square yards. Then think about how big that is.
1 yard is 3 feet. A square yard is 9 square feet. So nine sixteenths of a square yard is a bit more than 5 square feet.
Now she puts a fence 2 feet from the edge on each side. The plot is given in yards. The gap is in feet. Change to one unit.
Find the fence side, then its perimeter, then the area it encloses.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is the plot side in feet? How much do we add on both ends?

teaching_flow.title: Problem 3: curtains
teacher_says: Janet buys 5 yards of fabric. It is 1 and one half feet wide.
The length is in yards. The width is in feet. Change to the same unit.
She uses two fifths for a long set. The rest makes 4 short sets.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how much fabric is left after the long set? Then share it by 4.

teaching_flow.title: Problem 4: wire rectangles
teacher_says: Wire makes 3 rectangles, A, B and C. Each one is bigger than the one before.
Draw all three. Add to both sides of the rectangle each time.
The areas use fractions. You can use decimals too, if the fractions are in hundredths.
For wire, use perimeter. Wire goes around each rectangle.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what is added to the length? What is added to the width?

teaching_flow.title: Look back
teacher_says: Compare the problems. Did the distributive property or improper fractions help more?
Which problems were simple? Which were complex? What do they have in common?

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Draw it. Use one unit. Find each part. Check that the answer makes sense.

explanations.title: Area can be less than one
explanations.text: One side may be less than 1. Then the area can be less than one square unit. Picture one whole square tile. Only part of it is covered.

explanations.title: Square yards and square feet
explanations.text: One yard is 3 feet. A square yard is 3 feet by 3 feet, so it is 9 square feet. To change square yards to square feet, multiply by 9.

explanations.title: Use one unit
explanations.text: Some sizes may be in yards and some in feet. Change them all to one unit before you multiply. Feet are often easier.

explanations.title: Add on both ends
explanations.text: A fence is 2 feet out on every side. So each side gets 2 feet at both ends. That is 4 feet more on every side length.

explanations.title: Wire is perimeter
explanations.text: Wire goes around the edge of a shape. So wire is a length and uses perimeter. Area is the space inside and uses square units.

questions.text: A square is a rectangle with four equal sides. Is a square also a rhombus?
A flowerbed is 4 times as long as it is wide. The width is one third meter. How long is the flowerbed?
The bed is 4 thirds meters by one third meter. What is its area?
The bed needs 2 meter tiles to be as long as it is. Is its area less than 1 square meter?
A square basil plot is three fourths yard on each side. What is its area?
How many square feet are in 1 square yard?
The basil plot is 9 sixteenths of a square yard. What is that in square feet?
The plot is 2 and one fourth feet on each side. A fence is 2 feet away on every side. How long is one side of the fence square?
The fence square has sides of 6 and one fourth feet. What is the perimeter of the fence?
What is the area, in square feet, that the fence encloses?
Janet buys 5 yards of fabric. How many feet long is that?
The fabric is 15 feet long and 1 and one half feet wide. What is its area?
Janet uses two fifths of the fabric for the long curtains. How many square feet is that?
The rest of the fabric makes 4 short sets. What is the area of each short set?
Rectangle A is 2 cm by 1 and one half cm. B is one half cm larger on each side. C is one fourth cm larger than B. How long is the long side of C?
A is 3 square centimeters. B is 5 square centimeters. C is 2 and three fourths by 2 and one fourth. What is the total area of all three?
The wire for A, B and C is 7, 9 and 10 centimeters. A coil has 40 centimeters. How much wire is left?
When did the distributive property seem easier? When did improper fractions or decimals seem easier?
Which problems today were simple, and which were complex? What do they have in common?

objective.text: Draw trapezoids to clarify their attributes, and define trapezoids based on those attributes.

big_idea.text: A trapezoid is a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A polygon with four straight sides.
A quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides.
Lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet.
vocabulary.example: The two long sides of a ruler.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A trapezoid with two equal sides, the legs.
vocabulary.example: A trapezoid with equal slanted sides.

intro.hook: Shapes can be sorted by a rule, like toys by color.
intro.why_it_matters: A clear rule means everyone sorts the same way. Math needs clear rules.
intro.link_to_before: You know quadrilaterals, squares, rectangles and rhombuses.
intro.today_goal: Today you learn the rule for a trapezoid and use it to sort.

teaching_flow.title: A shape with a rule
teacher_says: Some shapes have four sides. Some have a special pair of sides that never meet.
Today we learn the rule for a trapezoid. Then we use it to sort shapes.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up: quadrilaterals
teacher_says: A quadrilateral is a polygon with four straight sides.
A square has four equal sides and four right angles. A rhombus has four equal sides. So a square is also a rhombus.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source shape sheet is a picture. The tutor uses words and one drawn shape.

teaching_flow.title: Sort quadrilaterals
teacher_says: Sort polygons by number of sides. Four sides make a quadrilateral.
Now sort quadrilaterals into trapezoids and non trapezoids. Look for parallel sides.
Parallel sides stay the same distance apart. They never meet.
A trapezoid has at least one pair of parallel sides. At least one means one or more.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: do any two sides stay the same distance apart?

teaching_flow.title: How the trapezoids are alike and different
teacher_says: All trapezoids have four straight sides. They are all quadrilaterals.
They can differ in side lengths and angles. Some trapezoids are rhombuses, rectangles or squares.
All of them have at least one pair of parallel sides.
A shape does not need to look like the usual trapezoid. The attribute decides.

teaching_flow.title: Draw a trapezoid
teacher_says: To draw one, first draw a pair of parallel lines. Then draw two more segments across them. The two segments must not cross each other.
Two trapezoids can be different. One may be a rectangle. One may be taller. One may have right angles. One may not.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source: children draw with a ruler and a set square. Not tutorable. The tutor describes the steps.

teaching_flow.title: Angles of a trapezoid
teacher_says: Label the angles A, B, C, D. A and B are at the top. C and D are at the bottom.
Cut the trapezoid between the parallel sides. Put angle A next to angle C. They make a straight line. That is 180 degrees.
Do the same with angles B and D. That is another 180 degrees. So there are two pairs.
Put all four angles together at a point. They go all the way around. That is 360 degrees.
Your measures may be close but not exact. Reading a protractor can be a little off.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what do two angles on a straight line add to? Then take away the angle you know.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The cutting is hands-on. The tutor describes it and the child answers.

teaching_flow.title: Isosceles trapezoid
teacher_says: An isosceles triangle has 2 equal sides. An isosceles trapezoid has 2 equal sides too. They are the legs.
To draw one: make a 5 cm base. Draw two 55 degree angles to make an isosceles triangle. Cut the top with a line parallel to the base.
The top angle of the triangle is 70 degrees. Each top angle of the trapezoid is 125 degrees.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what do the three angles of a triangle add to?

teaching_flow.title: Look back and check
teacher_says: When can a quadrilateral also be called a trapezoid? When it has at least one pair of parallel sides.
How can we check a shape? Use a ruler and a set square or right angle template. Use a protractor for angles.

teaching_flow.title: Review fractions of a set
teacher_says: Kathy spends three fifths of her money on a necklace. She spends two thirds of the rest on a bracelet. The bracelet costs 17 dollars.
Two fifths is left after the necklace. The bracelet is two thirds of that.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: This quick review is not about trapezoids. Ask it at the start if the child needs a warm up.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: A trapezoid is a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides. All trapezoids are quadrilaterals. Not all quadrilaterals are trapezoids.

explanations.title: What a trapezoid is
explanations.text: A trapezoid is a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides. At least one pair means one pair or two pairs. So rectangles, squares and rhombuses are trapezoids too.

explanations.title: Parallel sides
explanations.text: Parallel sides stay the same distance apart. They never meet, even if you extend them. A ruler and a set square help you check.

explanations.title: Angles of a trapezoid
explanations.text: Two angles on the same leg make a straight line. They add to 180 degrees. A trapezoid has two such pairs. All four angles add to 360 degrees.

explanations.title: The family of quadrilaterals
explanations.text: Every shape here is a quadrilateral. Trapezoids are inside it. Parallelograms, rectangles, rhombuses and squares are all inside the trapezoid group. Shapes with no parallel sides are outside it.

explanations.title: Isosceles trapezoid
explanations.text: An isosceles trapezoid has two equal sides, the legs. It is named after isosceles triangles, which also have two equal sides. Its base angles are equal.

examples.title: A rectangle is a trapezoid
examples.text: A rectangle has two pairs of parallel sides. A trapezoid needs at least one pair. So a rectangle is a trapezoid.

examples.title: Angles in a trapezoid
examples.text: Angle A is 65 degrees. Angle C is 115 degrees. Together they make 180. Angles of 70 and 110 make the other pair. All four add to 360.

examples.title: Drawing an isosceles trapezoid
examples.text: Base is 5 cm. Base angles are 55 degrees. Top angle of the triangle is 70 degrees. A cut parallel to the base gives top angles of 125 degrees.

objective.text: Draw parallelograms to clarify their attributes, and define parallelograms based on those attributes.

big_idea.text: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides. That gives it equal opposite sides and angles, and diagonals that bisect each other.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A flat shape with four straight sides.
Sides that never meet. They stay the same distance apart.
vocabulary.example: The two long sides of a ruler.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A four sided shape with two pairs of parallel sides.
Across from each other. Sides or angles that do not touch.
vocabulary.example: The top and bottom of a window.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A line joining two corners that are not next to each other.
vocabulary.example: A line from top left to bottom right.

vocabulary.kid_definition: To cut into two equal parts.
vocabulary.example: Cut a ribbon at its middle point.

intro.hook: Look around. Shelves, bridges and tiles use shapes with parallel sides.
intro.why_it_matters: Knowing the rules of a shape helps you draw it and check it.
intro.link_to_before: Yesterday we drew trapezoids with one pair of parallel sides.
intro.today_goal: Today we add a second pair and find the parallelogram rules.

teaching_flow.title: A leaning rectangle
teacher_says: Picture a rectangle that is pushed over at the top. It leans to one side.
The sides stay straight. The shape looks tipped. That is close to a parallelogram.
Today we find what is always true about parallelograms.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up: quadrilateral and trapezoid
teacher_says: A quadrilateral is any shape with four straight sides.
A trapezoid is a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides.
Parallel sides never meet. They stay the same distance apart.
Every shape we draw today starts with a pair of parallel lines. So each one is a trapezoid.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: In class students draw a pair of parallel lines with a ruler and set square. Here the tutor shows a picture instead.

teaching_flow.title: Draw a parallelogram
teacher_says: To make a trapezoid that is also a parallelogram, we need more.
Draw a second pair of parallel lines that cross the first pair.
Now both pairs of sides are parallel. That is a parallelogram.
A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides. Opposite sides are the same length.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: which side is across from AB? Opposite sides are the same length.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Class partners compare parallelograms. Some have right angles, some have four equal sides, some lean. Say that all of them still have two pairs of parallel sides.

teaching_flow.title: Angles in a parallelogram
teacher_says: Label the corners A, B, C and D going around. Measure each angle.
Opposite angles are equal. Angle A matches angle C. Angle B matches angle D.
Angles next to each other make a straight line. They add to 180 degrees.
There are four such pairs. All four angles together make 360 degrees.
Example: angle A is 60 degrees. Angle B is 120 degrees. Then 60 and 120 and 60 and 120 make 360.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: which two angles sit side by side on a straight line? What goes with 60 to make 180?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: In class students cut out the parallelogram, stack the angles and fit them together. Not possible here. Use the picture.

teaching_flow.title: Special cases and right angles
teacher_says: Some parallelograms have right angles. Some have none.
If one angle is a right angle, its neighbor is 90 degrees too. Then they all are.
So a parallelogram never has just one or just three right angles. It has none, or four.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Derived from the Exit Ticket drawing tasks. Extra explanation, not in the source.

teaching_flow.title: Diagonals of a parallelogram
teacher_says: A diagonal joins two corners that are not next to each other. A parallelogram has two.
Are they equal? Sometimes yes, sometimes no. A long leaning parallelogram has different diagonals.
Mark the crossing point O. The piece AO equals the piece OC. The piece BO equals the piece OD.
The diagonals bisect each other. Bisect means cut into two equal parts.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: is O in the middle of the diagonal? Then both pieces are equal.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Break the word. Bi means two, like two wheels on a bicycle. Sect means cut.

teaching_flow.title: Teresa's mistake
teacher_says: Teresa says one diagonal is 4.2 centimeters. So the other must be half of that.
Bisect cuts each diagonal in half. The pieces of the 4.2 diagonal are 2.1 each.
That says nothing about how long the other diagonal is.

teaching_flow.title: Sort the families
teacher_says: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides. So it fits the rule for a trapezoid, which needs at least one pair.
So all parallelograms are trapezoids. But a trapezoid with only one pair is not a parallelogram.
All parallelograms are quadrilaterals. A quadrilateral with no parallel sides is not a parallelogram.
A quadrilateral has four straight sides in one plane. The sides meet only at their ends.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Quadrilateral definition from the Debrief: four straight segments in one plane that meet only at their endpoints. If four segments cross in the middle, the figure is not a quadrilateral.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides. Opposite sides and opposite angles are equal.
Neighbor angles add to 180 degrees. All four add to 360 degrees. The diagonals bisect each other.

explanations.title: What a parallelogram is
explanations.text: A parallelogram is a quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides. It is also a trapezoid, because it has at least one pair.

explanations.title: Opposite sides and angles
explanations.text: In a parallelogram, opposite sides are the same length. Opposite angles are the same size. Neighbor sides can be different.

explanations.title: Angle facts
explanations.text: Neighbor angles add to 180 degrees. All four angles add to 360 degrees. If one angle is known, you can find all the others.

explanations.title: Diagonals bisect each other
explanations.text: The diagonals cross at their midpoints. Each is cut into two equal pieces. The two diagonals do not have to be equal.

explanations.title: The word bisect
explanations.text: Bi means two, like the two wheels of a bicycle. Sect means cut. So bisect means cut into two equal parts.

examples.title: Angles 60 and 120

examples.title: Angle 113 and its neighbor

objective.text: Draw rectangles and rhombuses to clarify their attributes. Define them by those attributes.

big_idea.text: A rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides. A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A parallelogram with four equal sides.
A parallelogram with four right angles.
Meeting at a right angle, 90 degrees.
A line that cuts another line in two equal parts at 90 degrees.
The point exactly in the middle of a line.
A line joining two corners that are not next to each other.
vocabulary.example: A line from corner to corner.

intro.hook: A kite, a door and a diamond on a card all have four sides.
intro.why_it_matters: Knowing what makes each shape special helps you name it and draw it.
intro.link_to_before: Yesterday we learned about parallelograms.
intro.today_goal: Today we learn two special parallelograms: the rhombus and the rectangle.

teaching_flow.title: Two special parallelograms
teacher_says: A diamond on a playing card has four equal sides. A door has four right angles.
Both are special parallelograms. Today we meet the rhombus and the rectangle.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up: cubes in a box
teacher_says: A box is 10 inches by 14 inches by 6 inches. We fill it with cubes with 2 inch edges.
Along the length, 10 divided by 2 gives 5 cubes. Along the width, 7 cubes. Along the height, 3 cubes.
Multiply the three counts to get the total.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source Application Problem reviews volume from earlier in the module.

teaching_flow.title: The rhombus
teacher_says: Yesterday we drew parallelograms. A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides.
A rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides.
To draw one, draw two equal sides from one corner. Then draw a line parallel to each side.
A rhombus can start from an acute angle or a right angle. Both give four equal sides.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: are all four sides the same? How many sides does a rhombus have? Divide the perimeter by that.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: In class students draw and measure. Here the tutor shows the picture.

teaching_flow.title: Rhombus angles
teacher_says: A rhombus is a parallelogram. So opposite angles are equal.
Neighbor angles make a straight line and add to 180 degrees.
Example: one angle is 70 degrees. Its neighbor is 110 degrees.

teaching_flow.title: Rhombus diagonals
teacher_says: Draw the diagonals. They bisect each other. The crossing point is the midpoint of both.
Now measure the angles where they cross. They are all 90 degrees.
Lines that meet at 90 degrees are perpendicular. So the diagonals are perpendicular bisectors.
The diagonals of a rhombus are not always equal. A tall thin rhombus has one long and one short diagonal. They are equal only in a square.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: do the diagonals meet at a right angle? Is the crossing point in the middle?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The source student line says rhombus diagonals are equal. That is true only for a square. Teach the corrected fact.

teaching_flow.title: Rhombus angle cases
teacher_says: A rhombus can have no right angles. It leans.
If a rhombus has one right angle, its neighbors are 90 degrees too. So all four are right angles. That is a square.

teaching_flow.title: The rectangle
teacher_says: A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles.
Opposite sides are parallel and equal. All angles are 90 degrees.
The diagonals are equal and bisect each other.
They do not cross at right angles, unless the rectangle is a square.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what size is each rectangle angle? Do the diagonals look equal?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: In class students cut and fold a rectangle to confirm angles and sides. Not possible here.

teaching_flow.title: Rhombus meets rectangle
teacher_says: A rectangle with four equal sides is a square. A rhombus with four right angles is also a square.
A parallelogram is a rectangle when it has four right angles.
A parallelogram is a rhombus when it has four equal sides.

teaching_flow.title: True or false
teacher_says: A rhombus is a parallelogram. So it is also a trapezoid. A trapezoid needs at least one pair of parallel sides.
A rectangle is a parallelogram and a trapezoid, too. But the reverse is not true. A trapezoid need not have right angles.
Now judge some statements.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source has eight true or false statements. These four are used. The other four (all rhombuses are trapezoids, all parallelograms are rectangles, all rectangles are parallelograms, all trapezoids are rhombuses) are covered in the says lines.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: A rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides. Its diagonals are perpendicular bisectors.
A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles. Its diagonals are equal and bisect each other.

explanations.title: What a rhombus is
explanations.text: A rhombus is a parallelogram with four equal sides. Opposite angles are equal. Neighbor angles add to 180 degrees.

explanations.title: Rhombus diagonals
explanations.text: The diagonals bisect each other and cross at 90 degrees. They are perpendicular bisectors. They are equal only if the rhombus is a square.

explanations.title: What a rectangle is
explanations.text: A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles. Opposite sides are equal. The diagonals are equal and bisect each other.

explanations.title: Special shape, big shape
explanations.text: A rhombus is a special parallelogram, so all rhombuses are parallelograms. Not all parallelograms are rhombuses. The special shape fits in the big one, never the other way.

explanations.title: Perpendicular bisectors
explanations.text: Perpendicular means meeting at a right angle. Bisector means cutting in two equal parts. Rhombus diagonals do both.

examples.title: Cubes in a box
examples.text: Along 10 inches fit 5 cubes. Along 14 inches fit 7. Along 6 inches fit 3. In all, 5 times 7 times 3 is 105 cubes.

examples.title: Perimeter 217
examples.text: A rhombus has a perimeter of 217 centimeters. All four sides are equal. Each side is 217 divided by 4.

examples.title: Rectangle diagonals
examples.text: A rectangle is 9 centimeters by 4 centimeters. Both diagonals are the same length. They cross at their midpoints but not at 90 degrees.

questions.text: A box is 10 inches long. Each cube has an edge of 2 inches. How many cubes fit along the length?
A box is 10 inches by 14 inches by 6 inches. How many 2 inch cubes fill it?
A rhombus is a parallelogram. How many of its sides are equal?
A rhombus has a perimeter of 217 centimeters. How long is each side?
One angle of a rhombus is 70 degrees. What is the angle next to it?
The diagonals of a rhombus cross. What size are the four angles where they cross?
What do we call two lines that meet at a right angle?
Rhombus diagonals cross at point O. AO is 6 centimeters. How long is OC?
Are the two diagonals of every rhombus the same length?
Can a rhombus have exactly one right angle?
Can a rhombus have no right angles at all?
How many right angles does a rectangle have?
A rectangle has two sides of 9 centimeters and two sides of 4 centimeters. Are its opposite sides equal?
Are the diagonals of a rectangle the same length?
Do the diagonals of a rectangle cross at right angles? The rectangle is not a square.
One diagonal of a rectangle is 10 centimeters. How long is the other diagonal?
A rectangle has all four sides equal. What is its other name?
When can a parallelogram also be called a rectangle?
True or false. All parallelograms are rhombuses.
True or false. All rhombuses are parallelograms.
True or false. All rectangles are trapezoids.
True or false. All trapezoids are rectangles.
What must a parallelogram have to be called a rhombus?

hints.text: Each cube has an edge of 2 inches. How many 2 inch pieces fit along the length?
A rhombus has four sides the same length. A parallelogram only needs opposite sides equal.
A perimeter is all four sides added. In a rhombus all four sides are the same.

misconceptions.label: Thinks the diagonals of a rhombus are equal
misconceptions.description: Child says rhombus diagonals have the same length. The source student line says this, but it is only true for a square. A rhombus has diagonals that bisect each other at 90 degrees.
detection_signals: child says rhombus diagonals are equal
child measures a square and says all rhombuses match
misconceptions.response_text: Picture a tall thin rhombus. One diagonal is long and one is short. They are equal only in a square. What is always true is that they cut each other in half at right angles.

misconceptions.label: Thinks rectangle diagonals cross at right angles
misconceptions.description: Child says the diagonals of a rectangle are perpendicular. They are equal and bisect, but they do not cross at 90 degrees unless the rectangle is a square.
detection_signals: child says the diagonals of a rectangle are perpendicular
child mixes up rhombus and rectangle diagonal facts
misconceptions.response_text: Rhombus diagonals meet at 90 degrees. Rectangle diagonals are equal in length. The rectangle diagonals lean, so the angles are not 90 degrees.

misconceptions.label: Thinks a rhombus cannot have right angles
misconceptions.description: Child says a rhombus is always slanted. A rhombus with right angles is a square. It is still a rhombus.
detection_signals: child says a rhombus cannot be a rectangle
child says a square is not a rhombus
misconceptions.response_text: A rhombus has four equal sides. It does not say anything about angles. If its angles are 90 degrees, it is a square. A square is still a rhombus.

misconceptions.label: Reverses a true statement

child says all parallelograms are rectangles

misconceptions.label: Thinks a rectangle cannot have equal sides
misconceptions.description: Child says a rectangle must have a long side and a short side. A rectangle with four equal sides is a square.
detection_signals: child says a square is not a rectangle
child says rectangle sides must differ
misconceptions.response_text: A rectangle needs four right angles. It does not need unequal sides. If all sides are equal, it is a square, which is still a rectangle.

objective.text: Draw kites and squares to clarify their attributes. Define them by those attributes.

big_idea.text: A square is a rhombus and a rectangle at once. A kite has two pairs of equal sides that touch.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A shape with four equal sides and four right angles.
A quadrilateral with two pairs of equal sides that touch each other.
Next to each other.
vocabulary.example: Two sides that share a corner.

vocabulary.kid_definition: Across from each other.
vocabulary.example: The top and bottom of a square.

vocabulary.kid_definition: Lines that cut each other in half at 90 degrees.
A line joining two corners that are not next to each other.
vocabulary.example: A line from corner to corner.

intro.hook: Floor tiles are squares. A kite in the sky is a different four sided shape.
intro.why_it_matters: Sorting shapes by their rules helps you name them and compare them.
intro.link_to_before: We have drawn rhombuses and rectangles.
intro.today_goal: Today we draw a square and a kite. Then we see how they fit.

teaching_flow.title: Square and kite
teacher_says: You know squares. You have also seen kites in the sky.
Today we see how a square fits with the rhombus and rectangle. Then we meet the kite.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up: Zach's question
teacher_says: Kylie drew a parallelogram. Zach says it is not a rectangle.
A parallelogram is a rectangle only if it has four right angles.
Zach is right if Kylie's shape has no right angles.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Kylie's Figure 1 and Zach's Figure 2 were pictures and were lost. The tutor uses the property instead.

teaching_flow.title: Draw a square
teacher_says: Draw a segment AB that is 3 inches long.
At A and at B, draw 3 inch segments straight down at 90 degrees. Call the ends D and C.
Both are at a right angle to AB. So they are parallel.
Join C and D. CD is also 3 inches. All four sides are equal and all four angles are 90 degrees.
That is a square.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: are the sides all 3 inches? Are the angles all 90 degrees? Which shape has both?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: In class students draw with a ruler and set square, and measure with a protractor. Not possible here.

teaching_flow.title: A square wears many names
teacher_says: Two pairs of parallel sides make a parallelogram. At least one pair makes a trapezoid.
Four right angles make it a rectangle. Four equal sides make it a rhombus.
So a square is a rectangle and a rhombus at the same time.
A square is a rectangle with four equal sides. It is a rhombus with four right angles.

teaching_flow.title: Square diagonals
teacher_says: Predict first. A square is a parallelogram, so the diagonals bisect each other.
Measure the pieces. They are equal. The diagonals do bisect each other.
They cross at right angles. So they are perpendicular bisectors.
A square is also a rectangle. So the diagonals are equal in length.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: what did we learn about rectangle diagonals? Is a square a rectangle?

teaching_flow.title: Meet the kite
teacher_says: A kite flies on a windy day on a string. Let us draw one.
Draw two equal sides from a point A. Fold to find the middle. Join to a point C on the fold.
A kite has two pairs of equal sides. The equal sides are next to each other, not across.
Opposite sides are not equal. No sides are parallel, in the kites we drew.
Example: sides 13 and 13 touch at A. Sides 20 and 20 touch at C.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: which two sides touch at A? Are they equal? Which pair touches at C?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: In class students fold, cut and measure. Here the tutor shows the picture.

teaching_flow.title: Kite angles and diagonals
teacher_says: A kite has at least one pair of equal angles. They are across from each other, where the unequal sides meet.
The diagonals meet at 90 degrees. They are perpendicular.
The diagonals are not equal. One diagonal cuts the other in half, but not both.
Some kites have diagonals that cross outside the shape. They are still perpendicular.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: are the two pieces of this diagonal equal? Which angles are across from each other?

teaching_flow.title: Can a kite be a parallelogram?
teacher_says: A kite needs sides next to each other that are equal. A rhombus has all four sides equal.
So every rhombus has equal sides next to each other. A rhombus is a kite. A square is a kite too.
These are the only parallelograms that are kites.
Jack says a square is not a kite because kites have no parallel sides. That is the error. Parallel sides do not matter for kites.

teaching_flow.title: True or false
teacher_says: Let us test the nesting. Think about special and general shapes.
Judge each statement.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: q_pr_13 (Kirkland) checks the formal quadrilateral definition: segments meet only at endpoints. Source has twelve statements. Six are questions here. All squares are quadrilaterals, all kites are quadrilaterals, all squares are parallelograms, and their reverses are in the explanations.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: A square has four equal sides and four right angles. It is a rhombus, a rectangle, a parallelogram, a trapezoid and a kite.
A kite has two pairs of equal sides that touch. Its diagonals are perpendicular.

explanations.title: What a square is
explanations.text: A square has four equal sides and four right angles. It is a rectangle with equal sides. It is a rhombus with right angles.

explanations.title: Square diagonals
explanations.text: The diagonals of a square bisect each other. They cross at 90 degrees. They are also equal in length.

explanations.title: What a kite is
explanations.text: A kite is a quadrilateral with two pairs of equal sides that touch each other. Opposite sides are not equal in most kites.

explanations.title: Kite diagonals and angles
explanations.text: The diagonals of a kite are perpendicular. One diagonal cuts the other in half. A pair of opposite angles are equal.

explanations.title: When a kite is a parallelogram
explanations.text: A kite is a parallelogram only when all four sides are equal. Then it is a rhombus. A square is also a kite.

explanations.title: Squares fit everywhere
explanations.text: A square is a quadrilateral, trapezoid, parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus and kite. Not all of those are squares. Special fits in general, not the other way.

objective.text: Classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties.

big_idea.text: Quadrilaterals sit in rings. A shape in an inner ring has every property of the rings around it.

vocabulary.kid_definition: Groups of shapes placed inside bigger groups.
A rule that is true about a shape.
vocabulary.example: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides.

vocabulary.kid_definition: The name of the innermost group a shape fits.
vocabulary.example: Square, for a shape with four equal sides and four right angles.

vocabulary.kid_definition: One drawing that shows a statement is false.
vocabulary.example: A parallelogram that is not a rectangle.

vocabulary.kid_definition: To cut into two equal parts.

intro.hook: Nesting dolls fit one inside another. Shapes fit like that too.
intro.why_it_matters: Sorting shapes helps you name them and prove true or false claims.
intro.link_to_before: We have met trapezoids, parallelograms, rectangles, rhombuses, squares and kites.
intro.today_goal: Today we sort them in one diagram and judge statements about them.

teaching_flow.title: Rings inside rings
teacher_says: Think of nesting dolls. A small doll sits inside a bigger doll.
Quadrilaterals work like that. Today we see which shapes sit inside which.

teaching_flow.title: Is it true?
teacher_says: We judge statements about shapes. We use their properties to decide.
Statement one. Trapezoids are always quadrilaterals. A trapezoid has four straight sides in one plane. So it is true.
Statement two. Quadrilaterals are always trapezoids. Many quadrilaterals have no parallel sides. So it is false.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: does every trapezoid have four sides? Does every quadrilateral have a pair of parallel sides?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: In class pairs draw shape name cards and fill a sentence frame. Here the tutor gives the frames.

teaching_flow.title: Place a trapezoid on the rings
teacher_says: The rings go outward: quadrilateral, trapezoid, parallelogram. Rectangle, rhombus and kite sit inside or beside them.
Take a shape with four sides and one pair of parallel sides.
It fits the quadrilateral ring and the trapezoid ring. It does not fit the parallelogram ring. A parallelogram needs two pairs.
Being in two rings means it has all the properties of both.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: how many pairs of parallel sides does the shape have? How many does a parallelogram need?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: In class students check properties with ruler and set square and glue shapes on the hierarchy. Not possible here.

teaching_flow.title: Properties pass inward
teacher_says: Use this frame. Because a shape is a trapezoid, it must have a trapezoid's properties.
Example: a rhombus is a trapezoid. So it has at least one pair of parallel sides.
Properties of a big ring belong to every shape inside it. The inner shapes have extra properties too.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: which ring is the shape in? What is the rule for that ring?

teaching_flow.title: True or false practice
teacher_says: Check the reverse each time. A special shape fits in the big one. The big one does not fit in the special one.
Rectangles are parallelograms. Parallelograms are not all rectangles.
A kite with four equal sides is a rhombus. So kites are sometimes rhombuses.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: draw a counter-example. Can you draw a parallelogram that is not a rectangle?
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Students can be challenged to draw counter-examples for each false statement.

teaching_flow.title: Many names for one shape
teacher_says: A square sits in every ring. It has seven names. Square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, trapezoid, kite and quadrilateral.
The most specific name is the innermost ring. The least specific is the outermost.
A rectangle has four names. A rhombus has five. A kite has two.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: which ring is the smallest one that holds the shape?

teaching_flow.title: Use properties to find numbers
teacher_says: A square has an area of 49 square centimeters. Each side is 7 centimeters. The perimeter is 28 centimeters.
The diagonals of a square bisect each other. One piece is 4.95 centimeters. So the whole diagonal is 9.9 centimeters.

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: A shape in an inner ring has the properties of every ring around it. Check statements by asking if the shape fits the rule.
Use the most specific name when you can.

explanations.title: The family rings
explanations.text: Quadrilateral is the biggest ring. Trapezoid sits inside it, then parallelogram. Inside parallelogram sit rectangle and rhombus. Square is where they overlap. Kite overlaps rhombus and square.

explanations.title: Properties pass inward
explanations.text: A shape in an inner ring keeps every property of the ring around it. It adds more properties of its own. A rhombus has parallel sides because it is a trapezoid.

explanations.title: Check the reverse
explanations.text: If all rectangles are parallelograms, the reverse is not true. Parallelograms include many shapes that are not rectangles. Draw a counter-example to prove a statement false.

explanations.title: Most and least specific
explanations.text: The outermost ring tells the least. The innermost ring tells the most. Four equal sides and four right angles? The most specific name is square.

explanations.title: Where the kite sits
explanations.text: A kite is a quadrilateral with two pairs of equal sides that touch. A rhombus has these, so it is a kite. A square is a kite. Most kites are in no other ring.

examples.title: A one-pair trapezoid
examples.text: A shape has four sides and one pair of parallel sides. It sits in the quadrilateral ring and the trapezoid ring. It is not a parallelogram.

examples.title: A square's names
examples.text: Square. Rectangle. Rhombus. Parallelogram. Trapezoid. Kite. Quadrilateral. That is seven names.

examples.title: Square with area 49
examples.text: Each side is 7 centimeters. The perimeter is 28 centimeters. A half diagonal of 4.95 means the whole diagonal is 9.9 centimeters.

A square has an area of 49 square centimeters. How long is each side?
What is the perimeter of that square?

hints.text: Look at the rings. A shape in an inside ring is also in every ring around it.
Everything true for a big ring is true for the shapes inside it. They just have more.
A parallelogram needs two pairs of parallel sides. This shape has only one pair.
Check the reverse. A special shape fits in the big one. The big one does not always fit in the special one.
A square is the most special shape. It sits in every ring.
The most specific name is the innermost ring the shape fits. The least specific is the outermost.
Count the rings the shape sits in. Count its own name as well.
Area of a square is side times side. Find the number that multiplied by itself gives 49.
Diagonals of a square bisect each other. The whole diagonal is two pieces.

misconceptions.label: Reverses a true statement
misconceptions.description: Child hears 'all rectangles are parallelograms' and says 'all parallelograms are rectangles'. The reverse is false.
detection_signals: child says all parallelograms are rectangles
child says all trapezoids are quadrilaterals so all quadrilaterals are trapezoids
misconceptions.response_text: Look at the rings. The rectangle ring sits inside the parallelogram ring. So all rectangles are parallelograms. The parallelogram ring has more shapes than the rectangle ring.

misconceptions.label: Thinks each shape belongs to only one family
misconceptions.description: Child gives one name only. A square is also a rectangle, a rhombus, a parallelogram, a trapezoid, a kite and a quadrilateral.
detection_signals: child says a square is only a square
child says a kite is never a rhombus
misconceptions.response_text: A shape can sit in many rings at once. Ask which rules the shape follows. Each rule it follows gives it another name.

misconceptions.label: Thinks inner shapes lose the properties of outer shapes
misconceptions.description: Child says a rhombus has no parallel sides because it is not a trapezoid. A shape in an inside ring keeps every property of the rings around it.
detection_signals: child says a rhombus is not a trapezoid
child says a square cannot be a trapezoid
misconceptions.response_text: A rhombus is a trapezoid. So it has at least one pair of parallel sides. It also has more. Properties pass inward.

misconceptions.label: Thinks the kite is totally separate from the other shapes
misconceptions.description: Child says kites are never rhombuses or squares. A rhombus or square has equal sides that touch, so it is a kite.
detection_signals: child says kites are never rhombuses
child says a square is not a kite
misconceptions.response_text: A kite needs two pairs of equal sides that touch. A rhombus has four equal sides, so it fits. A kite is a rhombus when all four sides are equal.

misconceptions.label: Mixes up most specific and least specific
misconceptions.description: Child gives quadrilateral as the most specific name for a square. The outer ring is the least specific.
detection_signals: child names the outer ring for most specific
child says quadrilateral for the most specific
misconceptions.response_text: The outer ring holds the most shapes, so its name tells the least. The innermost ring tells the most. For a square that is square.

recap_lines: A shape in an inner ring has every property of the rings around it.
Special shapes fit in general ones, never the other way.
A square fits in every ring.
Use the most specific name when you can.
wrap_up.mental_model: Inside rings: more specific, more properties.
wrap_up.closing_question: Say which shape sits in the most rings.

objective.text: Draw and identify varied two-dimensional figures from given attributes.

big_idea.text: Many shapes can fit the same clues. Name all of them and pick the most specific.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A fact about a shape, such as its sides or angles.
The name of the innermost group a shape fits.
vocabulary.example: Rectangle, for four right angles and unequal sides.

vocabulary.kid_definition: Next to each other.
vocabulary.example: Two sides that share a corner.

vocabulary.kid_definition: A quadrilateral with two pairs of parallel sides.
One drawing that shows a statement is false.
vocabulary.example: A trapezoid that is not a parallelogram.

intro.hook: A detective follows clues. Each clue rules out some shapes.
intro.why_it_matters: Reading clues about sides and angles helps you check which shape you have.
intro.link_to_before: We know all the quadrilaterals and how they nest.
intro.today_goal: Today we use clues to find shapes that fit.

teaching_flow.title: Detective shapes
teacher_says: Today you are a shape detective. I give you clues. You find shapes that fit.
Many shapes can fit the same clues. That is the fun part.

teaching_flow.title: Warm up: volume of two boxes
teacher_says: Volume of a box is length times width times height.
A composite solid can be split into two boxes. Find each volume. Then add.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: Source fluency. First box 6 by 3 by 2. Second box 7 by 2 by 2.

teaching_flow.title: Task: two pairs of equal sides
teacher_says: Task: draw a quadrilateral with two pairs of equal sides. Say as many names for it as you can.
Parallelograms have two pairs of equal sides across from each other. Rectangles and rhombuses and squares do too.
A kite has two pairs of equal sides that touch each other.
A trapezoid with only one pair of parallel sides cannot do it.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: do the equal sides sit across from each other or next to each other? Both can work.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: In class students draw their shape, compare with a neighbor and then six task cards each. Drawing is not tutorable here.

teaching_flow.title: Name it: most and least specific
teacher_says: Say I drew a rectangle. It is a rectangle, a parallelogram, a trapezoid and a quadrilateral.
Which name is the most specific? Rectangle. It is the innermost ring.
In class we circle the most specific name.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: which name tells the most about the shape?

teaching_flow.title: More tasks
teacher_says: Clues: four equal sides, no right angles. That is a rhombus.
Clues: four right angles, sides not all equal. That is a rectangle.
Clues: two pairs of equal sides that touch, no parallel sides. That is a kite.
A clue set can be impossible. Four equal sides and exactly one right angle cannot happen. One right angle makes all four right angles.
teaching_flow.teaching_note: The 24 task cards were stripped. These tasks are generated in the same style.

teaching_flow.title: John's error
teacher_says: John says rhombuses have no perpendicular sides. So he says they cannot be rectangles.
A rhombus can have right angles. Then it is a square. A square is also a rectangle.

teaching_flow.title: Jack's error
teacher_says: Jack says kites have no parallel sides. So a square is not a kite.
The kite rule is two pairs of equal sides that touch. A square has that. So a square is a kite.

teaching_flow.title: Always, sometimes or never
teacher_says: Always means every shape of the first kind fits the second. Sometimes means some do, some do not. Never means none do.
To say sometimes, give one example that fits and one that does not.
teaching_flow.if_child_is_stuck: Ask: can you find one shape that fits? One that does not?

teaching_flow.title: Recap
teacher_says: Clues can fit many shapes. Name every shape that fits. Circle the most specific.
Say always, sometimes or never. Use examples to prove it.

explanations.title: Many shapes, one task
explanations.text: A task lists a few rules. Any shape that follows all the rules is a correct answer. Different shapes can both be right.

explanations.title: Naming a shape
explanations.text: List every name that fits the shape. Then pick the name from the innermost ring. That is the most specific name.

explanations.title: Impossible clues
explanations.text: Some clue sets cannot be drawn. A rhombus with exactly one right angle is impossible. One right angle makes all four.

explanations.title: Always, sometimes, never
explanations.text: If every shape of one kind fits the other, say always. If none fits, say never. If some do and some do not, say sometimes. Show an example of each.

explanations.title: John and Jack
explanations.text: John forgot that a rhombus can have right angles. Then it is a square and a rectangle. Jack forgot that the kite rule only needs equal sides that touch.

examples.title: Shapes with two pairs of equal sides
examples.text: A rectangle fits. A rhombus fits. A kite fits. A trapezoid with one pair of parallel sides does not. The most specific name for a rectangle is rectangle.

examples.title: Two boxes joined
examples.text: First box 6 by 3 by 2 gives 36 cubic centimeters. Second box 7 by 2 by 2 gives 28 cubic centimeters. Together 64 cubic centimeters.

questions.text: A box is 6 centimeters by 3 centimeters by 2 centimeters. What is its volume?
A second box is 7 centimeters by 2 centimeters by 2 centimeters. It joins the first box. What is the volume of both together?
A task says: draw a quadrilateral with two pairs of equal sides. Could a rectangle be your answer?
Same task. Could a kite be your answer?
Same task. Could a trapezoid with only one pair of parallel sides be your answer?
Is there only one shape that is correct for this task?
I drew a rectangle. It is also a parallelogram, a trapezoid and a quadrilateral. How many names is that, counting rectangle?
Which of those names is the most specific?
A task says: four equal sides and no right angles. What is the most specific name?
A task says: four right angles and sides not all equal. What is the most specific name?
A task says: two pairs of equal sides that touch, and no parallel sides. What shape is it?
Can a quadrilateral have four equal sides and exactly one right angle?
John says rhombuses have no perpendicular sides, so they cannot be rectangles. Can a rhombus have perpendicular sides?
What do we call a rhombus that has right angles?
Jack says kites have no parallel sides, so a square is not a kite. Is a square a kite?
Is a kite a parallelogram? Say always, sometimes or never.
Is a trapezoid a parallelogram? Say always, sometimes or never.
Is a square a trapezoid? Say always, sometimes or never.
When is a trapezoid not a parallelogram?
When is a kite not a parallelogram?

hints.text: Volume of a box is length times width times height. Do each box, then add.
Equal pairs can be across from each other or next to each other.
Use the rings. Think of the shapes that have two pairs of equal sides.
Name every shape it fits. The most specific is the innermost ring.
A rhombus has four equal sides. It does not need right angles.
Neighbor angles in a parallelogram add to 180 degrees. One right angle makes all four.
Perpendicular sides mean a right angle. A rhombus with right angles is a square.
A kite needs two pairs of equal sides that touch. It says nothing about parallel sides.
To say sometimes, find one shape that fits and one that does not.
A trapezoid has at least one pair of parallel sides. A parallelogram has two pairs.

misconceptions.label: Thinks only one shape fits a task
misconceptions.description: Child thinks each task has one right drawing. Many shapes can follow the same attributes.
detection_signals: child says only a kite fits
child says only one shape has two pairs of equal sides
misconceptions.response_text: A task gives a few rules. Any shape that follows the rules is correct. Different shapes can all be right.

misconceptions.label: Gives a general name instead of the most specific
misconceptions.description: Child names a rectangle a quadrilateral and stops. All names are true, but the most specific is the innermost ring.
detection_signals: child circles quadrilateral
child lists one name only
misconceptions.response_text: List every name it fits. Then circle the one from the innermost ring. For a shape with four right angles and unequal sides, that is rectangle.

misconceptions.label: John: rhombuses have no perpendicular sides so cannot be rectangles
misconceptions.description: John thinks a rhombus always leans. A rhombus can have right angles. Then it is a square, and a square is a rectangle.
detection_signals: child says a rhombus is never a rectangle
child says rhombus sides are never perpendicular
misconceptions.response_text: A rhombus needs four equal sides. It may also have right angles. Then it is a square. A square is a rhombus and a rectangle.

misconceptions.label: Jack: kites have no parallel sides so a square is not a kite
misconceptions.description: Jack mixes up what a kite needs. The kite rule is two pairs of equal sides that touch. Parallel sides do not matter.
detection_signals: child says a square is not a kite
child says kites cannot have parallel sides
misconceptions.response_text: A square has four equal sides. So its equal sides touch. That meets the kite rule. Having parallel sides does not break it.

misconceptions.label: Says always or never when the answer is sometimes
misconceptions.description: Child says a kite is never a parallelogram, or a trapezoid is always one. One example in each direction shows sometimes.
detection_signals: child says a kite is never a parallelogram
child says all trapezoids are parallelograms
misconceptions.response_text: Find one kite that is a parallelogram, a rhombus. Find one that is not. That shows sometimes.

recap_lines: Clues can fit many shapes.
Name every shape that fits. Circle the most specific.
Some clues are impossible.
Say always, sometimes or never, and show an example.
wrap_up.mental_model: Clues are rules. Any shape that follows all the rules fits.
wrap_up.closing_question: Say what makes a rhombus also a rectangle.
